body: News Election Observers Say Kazakh President's Party Had 'Undue Advantage' As It Grabs 70 Percent Of Vote By Zamira Eshanova August 24, 2026 17:36 CET Election Observers Say Kazakh President's Party Had 'Undue Advantage' As It Grabs 70 Percent Of Vote Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Members of a local electoral commission count ballots at a polling station during parliamentary elections in Almaty, southeastern Kazakhstan, on August 23. Four months ago, the Adilet party did not exist. Today, it dominates Kazakhstan’s political landscape, following an election in which it gained 71.17 percent of the vote according to results announced on August 24. The vote marks a further tightening of President Qasym-Zhomart Toqaev's grip on power -- and was roundly criticized by international election observers from the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE). “The 23 August early parliamentary elections, while technically well prepared, took place in an environment lacking political pluralism. Political choice was reduced by the lack of distinct political alternatives, with all contesting parties supporting the incumbent President’s policies,” an OSCE statement said. In the August 24 statement , issued a day after the vote itself, the OSCE reported misuse of public resources, including public-sector employees being mobilized to attend campaign events, and concluded that Adilet had "an undue advantage that blurred the line between state and party.” The OSCE noted that independent candidates had been excluded from the election, a factor which “limited political participation and electoral competitiveness.” Observers also cast doubt on the results themselves, stating that discrepancies between what they saw at polling stations and official turnout data “raised questions about the integrity of the voter turnout reporting and the counting process.” OSCE missions have made similar criticisms of all previous elections held in Kazakhstan since it became independent after the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991, noting a lack of genuine political competition in an authoritarian country dominated for decades by presidents Nursultan Nazarbaev (1991-2019) and his successor, Toqaev. SEE ALSO: Kazakh Voters Appear To Approve Controversial Changes That Critics Say May Concentrate President's Power When Adilet was formed, in April, it absorbed the ruling party that had dominated Kazakhstan during and since the Nazarbaev era. Its stated aim is to implement Toqaev's policies and it will now comfortably control Kazakhstan's new unicameral parliament, the Kurultai. Adilet’s vote share was more than eleven times that of its nearest rival. The election was the first since constitutional changes rammed through by Toqaev earlier this year to switch from a previous bicameral structure. Media Pressure Before the Vote The election took place amid reports of pressure on independent activists and media. Almaty-based civil activist Asset Abishev said police blocked access to his home on August 23, which he described as interference with his right to vote. Another activist, Nurbol Arterkhan, who is under probation and subject to electronic monitoring, said he was repeatedly required to report to probation officials on election day and that police later visited his home. SEE ALSO: Criminal Cases, Travel Bans: Pressure Mounts On Kazakh Journalists Ahead Of Parliamentary Vote According to the Committee to Protect Journalists, five prominent journalists have been jailed or convicted since mid-July, while criminal cases have been opened against two others. Several have also been barred from practicing journalism. Media freedom was another major concern in the OSCE assessment. “Long-standing concerns about arrests and pressure on independent journalists generate pervasive self-censorship,” it noted in its statement. Sevilay Celenk, who headed a team of observers from the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE), also raised the issue. “Without an inclusive, credible, and pluralistic media environment, political participation and representation are fundamentally limited, especially during elections,” Celenk said. body: News Voting Over In Kazakh Election Amid Opposition Exclusion, Media Pressure By Zamira Eshanova and RFE/RL's Kazakh Service August 23, 2026 08:44 CET Voting Over In Kazakh Election Amid Opposition Exclusion, Media Pressure Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Voters cast their balots at a polling station during a snap parliamentary election in Almaty, Kazakhstan, on August 23. Kazakhstan has elected its new, unicameral parliament in a tightly controlled process following changes to the country's constitution, with genuine opposition groups excluded from the race. Seven state-vetted parties contested the election, while opposition groups were denied the status of political parties under legislation used to exclude them. The Central Election Commission said 72.15% of the more than 12.6 million voters on the electoral register had cast ballots by 6 p.m. local time. Preliminary results are expected on August 24. President Qasym-Zhomart Toqaev, whose reform agenda paved the way for the creation of the new unicameral parliament, cast his ballot at a polling station in Astana, calling the election an "important historic event" for Kazakhstan. He said the vote was only the beginning of a broader reform effort. Asked at the polling station whether he plans to seek another presidential term, Toqaev said it was too early to discuss the issue. His comments come after constitutional changes that have opened a legal path for him to seek another seven-year term. SEE ALSO: Is Political Opposition Still Possible In Central Asia? Toqaev also said there would be changes to the government following the election, without providing details. Under Kazakhstan's new constitutional system, the formation of a new parliament is expected to be followed by the resignation and re-formation of the government. The election took place amid reports of pressure on independent activists and media. Almaty-based civil activist Asset Abishev said police blocked access to his home on August 23, which he described as interference with his right to vote. Police did not immediately comment on the allegation. Another activist, Nurbol Arterkhan, who is under probation and subject to electronic monitoring, said he was repeatedly required to report to probation officials on election day and that police later visited his home. Arterkhan has previously faced prosecution over statements critical of the authorities. The restrictions extended to independent election monitoring. Under the election-monitoring rules, domestic nongovernmental groups receiving direct or indirect foreign funding cannot observe inside polling stations. This has left independent Kazakh watchdogs outside the official monitoring process. The authorities say 777 foreign observers are accredited, many representing regional organizations including the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO). The SCO said its observers had recorded no violations or complaints during the first half of voting on August 23. The SCO mission said it would issue its final assessment after polling, with a news conference scheduled for August 24. The OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR), whose interim report noted the absence of genuine opposition parties and independent candidates and concerns over restrictions on political expression, is also observing the vote. SEE ALSO: Criminal Cases, Travel Bans: Pressure Mounts On Kazakh Journalists Ahead Of Parliamentary Vote More than 70 parliamentarians and staff from around 30 countries were deployed as part of the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly observation mission, its 13th election observation mission in Kazakhstan since 1994. The OSCE has criticized all of the elections held in this period, noting a lack of genuine political competition in an authoritarian country dominated for decades by presidents Nursultan Nazarbaev (1991-2019) and his successor as head of state, Qasym-Zhomart Toqaev. The vote also took place amid pressure on independent media. According to the Committee to Protect Journalists, five prominent journalists have been jailed or convicted since mid-July, while criminal cases have been opened against two others. Several have also been barred from practicing journalism. The CEC is expected to release preliminary results on August 24, with final results due within seven days. Separately, the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR) will present its preliminary findings on August 24. The vote follows constitutional changes approved in a March referendum that replaced the previous bicameral parliament with a single chamber, the Kurultai. The Adilet party, which absorbed the former ruling party’s political structures as a new vehicle for the post-Nazarbaev era, is expected to dominate the first Kurultai. A nationwide poll by the Kazakhstan Institute of Public Development put the party at 70.2 percent support, positioning it to further cement Toqaev's grip on power. body: Kazakhstan Criminal Cases, Travel Bans: Pressure Mounts On Kazakh Journalists Ahead Of Parliamentary Vote By RFE/RL's Kazakh Service August 21, 2026 15:29 CET Criminal Cases, Travel Bans: Pressure Mounts On Kazakh Journalists Ahead Of Parliamentary Vote Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Journalists in Kazakhstan face growing legal and online restrictions, press freedom groups say. (file photo) Independent journalists and government critics in Kazakhstan are facing growing pressure ahead of parliamentary elections this weekend, rights groups say, pointing to criminal investigations, detentions, travel restrictions, and court-ordered bans on journalism. The vote on August 23 will elect the first members of the Kurultai, a new unicameral parliament that replaces Kazakhstan’s two-chamber legislature under constitutional changes approved in a March referendum. President Qasym-Zhomart Toqaev has portrayed the changes as political modernization. Critics say they have further concentrated power in the presidency, raising questions about the environment in which the first Kurultai election will take place. Adilet (Justice), a party founded in May and led by Toqaev’s former presidential administration chief, is heavily favored to win , with the latest national poll putting its support at 70.2 percent. The party absorbed the former ruling Amanat party and inherited its nationwide political network, leading critics to portray it as a rebranding of the pro-Toqaev political establishment. In an assessment last month of the upcoming vote, the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights said people interviewed by its mission had raised concerns about a “growing intolerance of criticism by the authorities, resulting in increasing pressure and sanctions.” They said this has contributed to “self-censorship and reduced civic participation.” Kazakh President Qasym-Zhomart Toqaev (file photo) On August 14, Civil Rights Defenders and eight other human rights and press freedom organizations warned of what they called a “broader, longer-term pattern” of politically motivated charges, online restrictions, and other forms of harassment and intimidation against government critics. The organizations highlighted four recent cases. Independent journalist and government critic Dinara Yegubaeva faces a criminal investigation following a July 31 traffic accident involving her car and a cyclist. Rights groups say the case was initially treated as an administrative matter. Authorities have also barred her from leaving Kazakhstan. Journalist and editor Lukpan Akhmedyarov is under investigation after sharing a Ukrainian government list of Kazakh citizens alleged to be fighting for Russia in Ukraine. Authorities accuse him of knowingly spreading false information. He was also barred from leaving Kazakhstan on August 3. Journalist Aleksandra Alyokhova, known by her pen name Sentsova, was convicted on August 3 of publishing private information about a person involved in a dispute at an Almaty bazaar. She received a three-year suspended prison sentence and was also barred from practicing journalism for three years. Rights groups say the information had previously been made public on a Telegram channel. Azamat Omarov (file photo) Political commentator Azamat Omarov, who runs the current affairs YouTube channel Akhual Segodnya, has been held in pretrial detention since July 18 on suspicion of inciting social, national, racial and religious discord. His lawyer says the case concerns videos containing satire and criticism of the authorities. Government Denies Crackdown The Kazakh government rejects allegations that it is suppressing legitimate journalism and criticism. Culture and Information Minister Aida Balaeva said on August 17 that the government does not block the social media accounts of journalists or media outlets. “The state is not interested in such actions or in restricting freedom of speech and opinion,” she said. “Combating unlawful content must not lead to unjustified restrictions...” Several recent court cases, however, have resulted in journalists being barred from their profession. KazTAG editor in chief Amir Qasenov On July 31, an Almaty court sentenced Amir Qasenov, editor in chief of KazTAG, an independent Kazakh news agency, to one year and three months of restricted freedom after convicting him of knowingly disseminating false information in articles about Freedom Finance, one of Kazakhstan’s largest brokerage firms. He was also banned from practicing journalism for five years. KazTAG’s general director Aset Mataev was convicted of failing to properly perform his managerial duties and of hooliganism in connection with a separate altercation in March. He received the same restricted-freedom sentence and three-year journalism ban. Both men denied the charges . Human rights activist Yevgeny Zhovtis said such restrictions have implications beyond professional journalism because bloggers and ordinary citizens also publish information and opinions online. “The approach here is not merely a ban on journalistic activity; its scope is much broader,” he said. “It amounts to depriving a person of their civil rights, specifically their freedom to express their opinion.” SEE ALSO: CPJ Expresses Concerns Over Kazakhstan's New Media Accreditation Rules Diana Okremova, director of Kazakhstan’s Legal Media Center, said bans on journalism were “completely incompatible” with democratic principles and Kazakhstan’s human-rights commitments. Another prominent independent journalist has been given a similar professional ban -- along with a lengthy prison sentence. On August 18, an Almaty court sentenced Gulnar Bazhkenova, former editor in chief of the news outlet Orda.kz, to eight years in prison and barred her from journalism and other activities for five years. Bazhkenova, who had been under house arrest since December, faced multiple charges, including repeatedly disseminating information that authorities claimed she knew to be false. She denied all the charges against her. Digital Restrictions Mount Press freedom monitors say the pressure has also increasingly moved online . RFE/RL’s Kazakh Service and Azattyq Asia, its Russian-language unit covering Central Asia, became difficult to access in Kazakhstan in May after RFE/RL published an investigation examining links between relatives of Toqaev and VD Stroy-Engineering, a recipient of large state contracts. Kazakh authorities denied involvement. Network measurements, however, found evidence consistent with deliberate restrictions on access. SEE ALSO: Access To RFE/RL Kazakh Websites Mysteriously 'Throttled' After Investigative Story The Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP) has separately documented what it described as fraudulent copyright complaints targeting RFE/RL content, including political coverage and investigations involving people allegedly linked to Kazakhstan’s political elite. Nazira Darimbet, head of the Adil Soz press freedom foundation, said online restrictions intensified around the March constitutional referendum, eased afterward, and have risen again ahead of the Kurultai election. “Sometimes we cannot even keep up,” she said. “This one is being blocked, that one is being blocked. Complaints are being filed against YouTube videos, and [journalists’ accounts] are being flagged for blocking.” The government denies responsibility for blocking journalists’ accounts. The August 23 vote will be the first nationwide election held under Kazakhstan’s new constitutional framework. SEE ALSO: Kazakh President Seeks Tighter Grip On Power With New Constitution The new constitution replaces the Senate and lower-house Mazhilis with the Kurultai and creates the post of vice president. The president appoints the vice president with parliamentary consent and continues to control key senior appointments. For T
summary: Independent journalists and government critics in Kazakhstan face mounting pressure ahead of the country’s first parliamentary elections following a controversial constitutional overhaul that critics say has strengthened the president’s power.
title: Criminal Cases, Travel Bans: Pressure Mounts On Kazakh Journalists Ahead Of Parliamentary Vote

body: Russia 'Organized Slavery': Russia's Tighter Migrant Rules Could Hit Central Asian Workers, Worsen Shortages By Azattyq Asia August 16, 2026 14:34 CET Listen 7 min This audio is automated Learn more 'Organized Slavery': Russia's Tighter Migrant Rules Could Hit Central Asian Workers, Worsen Shortages Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google About 3 million foreigners were working in Russia at the beginning of 2026, many of them from Central Asian countries. (file photo) Russia is proposing an overhaul of its system for recruiting foreign workers beginning in 2027, tying migrants to specific employers, jobs, and regions in a move authorities say will give the state greater control over labor migration. But the plan is already drawing concern from migration experts and businesses. They warn that tighter restrictions could drive migrant workers into informal employment and further worsen workforce shortages in a country that relies heavily on foreign labor. The four-year experiment, scheduled to run from January 1, 2027, through the end of 2030, would cover 87 Russian regions, excluding Moscow and the Moscow region. Russian authorities estimate that more than 1.7 million foreign workers could be affected, including large numbers from Central Asia. The new system would move away from the “work-patent” mechanism that has been the main route to legal employment for migrants from visa-free countries such as Uzbekistan and Tajikistan. In 2025, foreigners obtained about 2.3 million Russian work patents, according to Interior Ministry figures. That represented more than 40 percent of all foreigners in Russia and almost 77 percent of officially employed foreign workers. SEE ALSO: Central Asian Schoolchildren Caught Up In Russia's Crackdown On Migrants Russia remains heavily dependent on foreign labor. About 3 million foreigners were officially working in the country at the beginning of 2026, while the total number of foreign nationals in Russia, including migrants’ family members, exceeded 5.7 million, according to the ministry. Under the proposed system, migrants would arrive in Russia already matched with a particular employer and vacancy. A new information system would maintain registries of employers and foreign workers and match workers with jobs based on regional labor-market needs. The system would also expand the amount of information authorities collect on migrants before they enter Russia. In addition to photographs and fingerprints, migrants would undergo mandatory genomic registration and medical examinations. 'No Rights For The Migrant' For migrants, however, the biggest change could be the loss of freedom to change jobs. Under the proposed rules, once in Russia, workers recruited through the new system would not be allowed to work for a different employer, in a different profession, or outside the region specified in the registry until their employment contracts expire. SEE ALSO: Russia's Migrant Crackdown Expands With Mandatory Mobile Tracking Violating those rules could result in removal from the foreign-worker registry and an obligation to leave Russia. Such workers could then only reenter the system and regain the ability to work in Russia after a year. “During my nearly 15 years in Russia, I have always stayed in the same city, but I changed my work several times with different private construction companies, depending on the money and conditions they offered,” Sarvar, a Tajik worker in the Russian city of Surgut, told RFE/RL. “I don’t know much about this plan yet, but I fear that if my employer knows that I can’t easily change my job, it would be difficult for me to negotiate my salary or other things.” A Russian traffic policeman checks the documents of guest workers from Central Asia. (file photo) Valentina Chupik, a human-rights advocate who heads Tong Jahoni, an organization that assists migrants, said the restrictions could leave workers particularly vulnerable to abusive employers. “There will be no rights for the migrant. He will be firmly attached to the employer,” Chupik said, describing the proposed system as “organized slavery.” The government says the new model is intended to make migration more transparent and reduce illegal employment by giving authorities more information about workers before they arrive. It also says the model is intended to increase employers’ responsibilities. Divided Opinion The proposed changes have divided migration experts. Mikhail Burda, head of the Center for Migration Studies at the Moscow-based Tsargrad Institute, argues that the country will remain attractive because of the size of its labor market and its established ties with Central Asia. “Targeted organized recruitment should become the only possible procedure for temporary employment in Russia for mass migration,” Burda said. “The formula ‘come, work, leave’ should be implemented in its absolute sense, without reservations or exceptions.” SEE ALSO: Thousands Of Central Asians Enlisted To Fight Russia's War In Ukraine Through 'Coercion, Enticements' Karimjon Yorov, a Tajik migration expert, takes a sharply different view. He said the additional procedures and restrictions could make it harder for Central Asian workers to enter Russia. “I can say with confidence that there is nothing good in it,” Yorov said. “Unfortunately, the consequences will be bad...for all migrants.” Yorov warned that the new recruitment system could create opportunities for corruption if intermediaries begin charging migrants for access to jobs or recruitment lists. He recalled that when work permits cost 1,000 to 2,000 rubles ($12-$24 at current exchange rates), they were sometimes resold for 20,000 to 50,000 rubles ($240-$600). Russia’s business community is also worried about the potential consequences. The Russian Union of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs has warned the government that tying migrants to a single employer could push some workers out of the formal economy. The group wants migrants to be allowed to work for multiple employers and for the process of changing jobs to be made easier. The business group has also proposed delaying the experiment from 2027 to 2028 and introducing a two-year transition period during which the new system would operate alongside existing patent and work-permit mechanisms. Moscow has begun reviewing its agreements with Uzbekistan and Tajikistan, two major sources of migrant labor, on organized recruitment. Yorov told RFE/RL that Tajikistan has begun preparing for the new system, with centers being established to prepare prospective migrants and conduct medical examinations, fingerprinting, and photography. Written by Farangis Najibullah based on reporting by Azattyq Asia. summary: Russia is proposing an overhaul of its foreign-worker recruitment system in 2027, tying migrants to specific employers, jobs, and regions. Experts warn that tighter rules could worsen labor shortages and push more migrants into informal employment.
title: 'Organized Slavery': Russia's Tighter Migrant Rules Could Hit Central Asian Workers, Worsen Shortages

body: News Amid Setbacks, Putin Looks To Restore Russia's Standing At Bishkek SCO Summit By RFE/RL August 31, 2026 00:43 CET Listen 6 min This audio is automated Learn more Amid Setbacks, Putin Looks To Restore Russia's Standing At Bishkek SCO Summit Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Russian President Vladimir Putin (right) and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi shake hands during a meeting on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Bishkek on August 31. Facing increasing confrontations with the West, Russian President Vladimir Putin is looking eastward to restore his country's standing in the region at a major summit in Bishkek, the Kyrgyz capital. It comes at a time of increased difficulties for the Kremlin leader, with Russia's economy in tatters due to Western sanctions and Ukrainian drone strikes, ally Iran battered in war, and the leaders of former client states such as Syria and Venezuela ousted amid a muted Moscow response. Putin is set to hold bilateral meetings with at least nine world leaders, including Iranian President Masud Pezeshkian, starting on August 31 on the sidelines of the two-day Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO), which is celebrating its 25th anniversary. SEE ALSO: Aggressive Recruiters Are Rounding Up Russians To Fight In Ukraine. In One Town, They're Pushing Back On the first day, the Russian leader met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Putin and Xi focused on bilateral issues and only discussed the war in Ukraine "marginally...essentially there was no discussion." Western nations have called on China to use its influence to pressure the Kremlin into ending its war on Ukraine. Russia's Interfax news agency reported Modi told Putin that India supported "every peace effort" to end the war in Ukraine, without providing further details. Putin is also expected to hold bilateral sessions with leaders of non-SCO nations, including Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinian, who has angered the Kremlin by seeking closer ties to the West for his small Caucasus nation. United Front Putin and Xi have often used SCO gatherings to put up a united front against Western influence in the region. Xi arrived late on August 30 and held his first meeting with Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov, who will serve as host of the summit. Along with Russia, Iran, India, and China, the SCO grouping consists of Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan, Uzbekistan, and Tajikistan. Not all members are allies, of course, with nuclear powers Pakistan and India often on the brink of war with each other. Russian President Vladimir Putin and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi greet each other on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in Bishkek on August 31. The organization began as the "Shanghai Five" in 1996 but began expanding to other regional nations starting in 2001. Moscow and Tehran are both under crippling Western sanctions -- Russia for its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 and Iran for a multitude of issues, including its support for extremist activity in the Middle East and its alleged pursuit of a nuclear weapon. Kyiv and the West have demanded Iran cease from providing deadly Shahed drones to Russia for use in the Ukraine war, while US officials told RFE/RL that Russia is providing Iran with targeting information to attack US troops and military assets in the Middle East, confirming a Washington Post report . 'Key Subjects' Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov said "one of the key subjects" in the talks between Putin and Pezeshkian will be the Middle East crisis. "You know how relevant this meeting is in light of the current uneasy atmosphere in the Middle East and the situation surrounding Iran," he added. Also on the agenda will be the $25 billion agreement signed by Tehran with Russia's state nuclear company Rosatom to build four nuclear power plants in Iran. Leaders of SCO nations attend the 2025 summit in the Chinese city of Tianjin. Naser al-Tamimi, a UK-based analyst and founder of MidEast Strategia, wrote on X that the SCO can help largely isolated Iran, "but only to a point." "The SCO offers Iran broader political cover, helps reduce its international isolation, and expands opportunities for trade and settlements in yuan, rubles, and other national currencies. In doing so, it can modestly reduce Tehran's dependence on the Western financial system." "But the SCO is not an economic shield against US sanctions. It lacks a fully developed alternative financial architecture, provides no reliable protection for major banks and companies exposed to secondary sanctions, and cannot compel China or India to absorb high economic costs on Iran’s behalf." Potentially Tense Armenian Meeting Along with Turkey, other nonmember nations and others participating and observing will include Armenia, Azerbaijan, UN chief Antonio Guterres, and heads of several Moscow-oriented international organizations. Putin is scheduled to meet Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinian, whose country has long been an ally of Russia but which has angered Moscow by seeking to move closer to the West. SEE ALSO: Mobilization Migration: Is There An Uptick In Russians Fleeing Amid Fears Of A New Draft? Tensions heightened between the two countries after Armenian police on August 25 arrested former President Robert Kocharian, now leader of the country's second-largest opposition party, amid accusations of corruption-related offenses. Kocharian, 71, served as Armenia's president between 1998 and 2008. He currently leads the Armenia Alliance, which is considered pro-Moscow and finished third in recent parliamentary elections in June. Yerevan has also angered Moscow by expressing its ambition to eventually join the European Union. SEE ALSO: Former Armenian President Arrested On Corruption Charges "We will insist that Armenia cannot aspire for EU membership while hugely benefiting from cooperation within the European Economic Union (EEU)," said Ushakov, referring to the five-member trade bloc that also includes Belarus, Kazakhstan, and Kyrgyzstan. Following the Bishkek event, Putin is scheduled to travel to Vladivostok for the Eastern Economic Forum on Russia's Pacific coast from September 1-4. He is also set to meet with leaders of several other countries there, including the Indonesian president and Mongolian prime minister. body: Russia Mobilization Migration: Is There An Uptick In Russians Fleeing Amid Fears Of A New Draft? By Ray Furlong , Robert Zargaryan , Sandro Jupalakiani and Zamira Kozhobaeva August 21, 2026 14:46 CET Mobilization Migration: Is There An Uptick In Russians Fleeing Amid Fears Of A New Draft? Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Sergei Rasokhin talking to RFE/RL's Armenian Service, August 7, 2026 Sergei Rasokhin says he spent two years in hiding before finally escaping military service in Russia and recently making it to safety in Armenia. The country took in many Russians dodging the draft in 2022-23 and now, amid growing fears of a new mobilization in Russia to boost a military depleted by the war on Ukraine, there are some indications that the numbers of Russians coming to Armenia are again rising. There have also been recent signs of this in other countries that saw an influx of Russians in 2022-23, but the evidence is patchy and sometimes conflicting. SEE ALSO: 'No Way Out': Russia Sends Badly Wounded Men Back Into Battle In Ukraine In any case, if the Kremlin decides to announce a new wave of mobilization, it may wait until after parliamentary elections next month -- meaning those hoping to avoid it still have time. Two Years In Hiding Rasokhin told his story to RFE/RL’s Armenian Service from the safety of Yerevan, home to a thriving community of Russians who have fled the increasingly repressive environment in their homeland under President Vladimir Putin in recent years. He said his life changed completely two years ago when, to deal with financial problems, he voluntarily signed a contract to join the Russian Army. He was told he would serve as an auto mechanic -- but soon learned he’d been tricked. “The sergeant laughed at me. He said: ‘You were deceived. They will take you to the front line with 95 percent certainty. Don’t hope for anything else,’” Rasokhin said. Rasokhin said he ran away from his unit and spent two years on the run, moving on from one location to another every few months, until he was eventually captured by military police. SEE ALSO: Russia Scrambles To Recruit Enough Men For Ukraine War. Now It’s Also Forcing Them. Instead of taking up arms, Rasokhin said he preferred to stand trial, even though he knew that deserters face up to 15 years in prison. Awaiting trial, he decided to buy a train ticket to Belarus. “[People] advised me to buy a ticket in cash an hour before departure, so that they wouldn’t have time to check the details. When I was at the ticket office, a man in an armed forces uniform came and took some papers. As I understood it, it was the list of passengers with tickets. And I hadn't bought one yet at that point, so maybe that saved me," he said. Rasokhin said he hoped his story would inspire other Russians to know that there are ways to get out of the country and avoid military service. What Do The Numbers Show? Official statistics show an uptick of Russians entering Armenia. Following the declaration of mobilization in September 2022, more than 500,000 Russians came to Armenia on tourist visas in the first six months of 2023. Every year after, the numbers fell, reaching nearly 340,000 last year. But between January and June this year they’re up again -- at some 417,000 people. Of course, this by itself does not prove an exodus. People, especially tourists, come and go. Another indicator is how these numbers compare. An outlier compared to statistics for previous years, this is a fairly large number given that, according to official data from December last year, the total of Russian citizens with Armenian residence permits was 43,000 people. An increase in people staying in Armenia would put pressure on the housing markets, and there’s anecdotal evidence of this. Back in July, an independent Russian media outlet, Vyorstka , cited real estate agents in Yerevan talking of a sharp increase in demand from Russians. This was confirmed by real estate agents that spoke to RFE/RL’s Armenian Service, though most declined to be quoted. One agent, who agreed to identified by his first name, Gevorg, said: “Based on my impression and my local statistics -- there is about a 30 percent increase in prices. Up to a 50 percent jump in the case of rentals.” It was, he said, “very similar to 2022.” The change in market conditions is doubly interesting given that it reverses a previous trend, identified by another independent Russian outlet, The Insider , in July. “By 2025, the rental market had stabilized. Experts note a 30 percent decline in rates compared to the peak at the start of the full-scale war,” it said. In other words, it appears the market is again on a sharp upward curve -- possibly driven or partly-driven by new arrivals from Russia. What About Other Countries? Back in 2022-23, Russians were also fleeing to other countries. Dramatic drone footage revealed enormous lines of traffic at the border with Georgia, for example. On August 18, official Russian data made headlines by reporting that more than 20,000 people had crossed the main crossing into Georgia on a single day. It added that a “similar dynamic” had been observed for several days. This "significantly exceeds the data for the same period in previous years," it said. The Georgian authorities denied the Russian claim, however. In a statement on August 19, it said some 7,900 citizens had used the crossing to enter Georgia in 24 hours beginning at 9 a.m. on August 18. SEE ALSO: 'The Country Is In Trouble. When Will You Return?': Russians Fleeing To Georgia Share Their Experiences Of Getting Out There may be some discrepancy on what 24-hour period the two datasets refer to, but in any case the situation is unclear. When RFE/RL’s Georgian Service visited the border crossing on August 20, they saw no evidence of mass traffic jams or an exodus of fleeing Russians. "I came in 2022, and back then people were waiting for days. Today, when we went through, there were only three or four cars ahead of us on the Russian side," one young Russian woman said after driving across the border. There have also been anecdotal reports from Central Asia of dual-nationals returning from Russia due to fears of an imminent military draft. RFE/RL’s Kyrgyz Service spoke to a woman who declined to be identified for security reasons. She lived in Russia for more than 20 years, gaining citizenship for herself and her children. “When I heard that there would be a mass mobilization in the fall, the first thing I thought about was my son, who was already in his 20s, and we returned to our homeland,” she said. SEE ALSO: Anti-War Russians Abroad Fear Kremlin Covertly Pressuring Hosts To Send Them Back A representative of a Kyrgyz diaspora group in Russia, who could not be named for security reasons, said cases like this were on the rise. "Kyrgyz people are leaving Russia for other places, including Kyrgyzstan, due to various pressures. There is also development and job creation in Kyrgyzstan, so many people are leaving for there,” he said. “Recently, when an acquaintance of mine with Russian citizenship was leaving for Kyrgyzstan, he was warned at the border that ‘if you don't come back, your house and property here will be confiscated.’ Some of them, even if they have citizenship, say they won't come back. They sell their houses and leave," he added. But, he said, other dual nationals were staying, having been rejected for military service in the previous mobilization for health or other reasons. summary: Armenia and other countries bordering Russia took in many Russians dodging the draft in 2022-23 and now, amid growing fears of a new mobilization to boost a military depleted by the war on Ukraine, there are some indications that the numbers of Russians coming to Armenia are again rising.
title: Mobilization Migration: Is There An Uptick In Russians Fleeing Amid Fears Of A New Draft?

body: Uzbekistan Uzbekistan's Saida Mirziyoeva Gains New Powers, Fueling Succession Questions By Farangis Najibullah and Khiromon Baqozoda August 22, 2026 11:09 CET Listen 7 min This audio is automated Learn more Uzbekistan's Saida Mirziyoeva Gains New Powers, Fueling Succession Questions Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Saida Mirziyoeva (file photo) When Saida Mirziyoeva entered Uzbekistan's government in 2019, she was largely unknown and had no previous political experience. Seven years later, the eldest daughter of President Shavkat Mirziyoev has become one of the most powerful people in the country and a figure increasingly discussed as a possible successor to her father. A law signed by Mirziyoev on August 14 has given that speculation a new dimension by formally expanding the powers of the Presidential Administration, which Mirziyoeva, 41, heads. Under the law, the head of the administration -- the president's chief of staff -- becomes deputy chair of the Security Council, which is headed by the president and coordinates the country's security, law enforcement and military structures. Mirziyoeva will also organize and coordinate the activities of the council's members. Alisher Ilhomov, a London-based Central Asia analyst, said the change is particularly significant because control over the security apparatus is one of the main pillars of the president's power. "She was already de facto the No. 2 person in the country after the president, but her position was not strongly regulated by law. Now a legal foundation has been created that allows her to concentrate power and control over the security agencies," Ilhomov said. The new powers are the latest step in a rapid political rise that has repeatedly fueled speculation that Mirziyoev could be preparing his daughter for the presidency. Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoev (fourth from right) and members of his family pose while voting in a presidential election in July 2023. Mirziyoev, 69, won a third term in a tightly scripted election in 2023, while being awarded 87 percent of the vote. The same year, he engineered a constitutional overhaul that extended the presidential term to seven years and gave him the right to run again in 2030, meaning he could rule until 2037. Mirziyoeva joined the government in April 2019 as deputy head of the Agency for Information and Mass Communications, a position that also made her a deputy presidential adviser. SEE ALSO: Uzbekistan's Increasingly Influential First Daughter Seen As Successor To President Mirziyoev In 2020, she became deputy chair of the supervisory board of the Public Foundation for Support and Development of National Mass Media. In November 2022, she was appointed head of the Communications and Information Policy Department in the Presidential Administration, placing her at the center of the government's media and public relations strategy. Then, in August 2023, Mirziyoeva was appointed first assistant to the president, effectively becoming the second highest-ranking official in the Presidential Administration after the president. At the time, independent Uzbek journalist Jahongir Muhammad described her rise as "meteoric." "A literally unknown person got the second-highest post in Uzbekistan out of the blue," he said. High-Profile Responsibilities In June 2025, Mirziyoev restored the position of head of the Presidential Administration and appointed his daughter to the post, further consolidating her position at the center of the government. Saida Mirziyoeva and Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin in Moscow in May 2025 Mirziyoeva has since taken on additional high-profile responsibilities. In November 2025, she was appointed Uzbek co-chair of the newly established American-Uzbek Business and Investment Council. The appointment gave Mirziyoeva a prominent role in managing a major channel of Uzbekistan's economic relations with the United States. There has been no official indication that Mirziyoeva is being prepared to succeed her father. But her expanding role has also revived comparisons with Gulnara Karimova, the daughter of Islam Karimov, who was Uzbekistan's president from 1990, before the Soviet Union's collapse, until his death in 2016. SEE ALSO: Gulnara Karimova Enjoying 'Special Treatment' In Uzbek Prison, Former Inmate Says Karimova was once viewed as a possible successor to her father before falling out with him and eventually being imprisoned. But unlike Karimova, Mirziyoeva has steadily accumulated formal government positions. Sweeping Authority The latest law goes further by giving the office Mirziyoeva heads sweeping authority over government bodies and state institutions. The Presidential Administration can monitor and coordinate the work of government agencies and regional authorities, evaluate officials, issue instructions, and make proposals on domestic and foreign policy. It has also now acquired a role in coordinating the work of law enforcement and security structures. The law has drawn particular attention for its broad immunity provisions. Some senior Presidential Administration officials will retain immunity for life after leaving office, while other managerial officials will retain it for five years. The protections extend to their homes, vehicles, correspondence, and electronic data, and place significant restrictions on criminal investigations and other procedural measures against them. Mirziyoeva during a visit to Uzbekistan's Andijon region in June. Shukhrat Latipov, a journalist with the independent Uzbek outlet Gazeta.uz, questioned the breadth of the immunity provisions in the new law, writing on Telegram that they raised questions that required additional public explanation. "I don't know whether employees and heads of other presidential administrations around the world have such guarantees," Latipov wrote. Latipov also questioned how quickly the law was adopted. The lower legislative house approved it on August 6, the Senate on August 7, and Mirziyoev signed it on August 14, a remarkably short period for legislation of this significance, Latipov noted. For Ilhomov, however, the most consequential change is the formal role Mirziyoeva now has in the security structures. SEE ALSO: A New Uzbek Princess? The Growing Stature Of The President's Daughter Raises Eyebrows In Uzbekistan He said the new law potentially puts her in a position to help control the security agencies that are central to maintaining political power. That does not necessarily mean Mirziyoev is preparing to hand over the presidency anytime soon, or to tip his daughter as his chosen successor when his current term ends in 2030. Ilhomov said the new arrangement should instead be viewed as a kind of backup system, a way to ensure that a trusted figure can maintain control of the state if unexpected developments prevent Mirziyoev from doing so. "It is being done in case of a possible change of power under some extraordinary circumstances," Ilhomov said. She has extensively covered efforts by Central Asian states to repatriate and reintegrate their citizens who joined Islamic State in Syria and Iraq. summary: A new law expanding the powers of Uzbekistan’s Presidential Administration has further elevated Saida Mirziyoeva, the president’s daughter, within the country’s political hierarchy. It gives her a role in the Security Council and has fueled fresh speculation about Uzbekistan’s eventual succession.
title: Uzbekistan's Saida Mirziyoeva Gains New Powers, Fueling Succession Questions

(file photo) Iran live Oil Hits 4-Month High As Hormuz, Red Sea Risks Mount September 11, 2026 07:15 CET Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google As the conflict in the Persian Gulf continues to impact and shape the region, journalists from RFE/RL's Central Newsroom and Iranian service, Radio Farda, deliver ongoing updates and analysis. Key Takeaways Oil prices surged to a four-month high on September 11 amid fears of prolonged supply disruptions and renewed inflation. US President Donald Trump said he had no regrets about going to war with Iran despite the conflict's potential impact on November's midterm elections Gulf Arab foreign ministers are expected to meet Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi in Oman next week as regional powers seek support for a temporary arrangement to restore commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian President Masud Pezeshkian arrived in New Delhi on September 11 for a BRICS summit, with the escalating Middle East conflict expected to feature prominently. Several US military aircraft were damaged in Iranian missile strikes on a base in Jordan housing American soldiers, according to reports. New posts 14:24 Houthis Reach Strategic Island On Key Red Sea Shipping Route Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi rebels have reached the strategic island of Perim, also known as Mayyun, in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, potentially strengthening their grip on one of the world's most important shipping routes, according to Yemeni government sources. Four government sources told Reuters on September 11 that Houthi forces had reached the island, while the German dpa news agency cited a Yemeni government source as saying the group had taken control of it. Reuters reported that forces loyal to Yemen's internationally recognized government had withdrawn from Perim. AFP cited an unnamed Yemeni military official as saying the Houthis now control the country's entire Red Sea coast. All territory that had been under government control "on the western coast has fallen" following the Houthis' seizure of Perim and the Greater and Lesser Hanish islands, AFP quoted the military official as saying. Perim, or Mayyun, sits at the southern entrance to the Bab al-Mandab, the narrow waterway connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and a crucial route for trade and energy shipments between Asia and Europe via the Suez Canal. The waterway's strategic importance has grown sharply since the Iran war disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, another of the world's key energy chokepoints. The Houthi advance follows the group's reported capture of the Red Sea port of Mocha on September 10. Government sources also reported Houthi advances on the mainland and other islands in the strait. The developments raise the prospect of disruptions to shipping through the Red Sea at a time when Saudi Arabia has become increasingly reliant on the route for oil exports because of conflict-related restrictions in the Strait of Hormuz. Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share 11:54 Iranian President Arrives In New Delhi For BRICS Summit Amid Gulf Crisis Iranian President Masud Pezeshkian (center right) arrives to attend a BRICS summit in New Delhi on September 11. Iranian President Masud Pezeshkian arrived in the Indian capital, New Delhi, on September 11 to join the leaders of BRICS countries for a summit, with the escalating Middle East conflict expected to feature prominently on the agenda. BRICS, a grouping of major emerging markets and developing countries, takes its name from Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa. It expanded from five to 11 members in 2024 and 2025, adding Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Making his first visit to India since taking office in 2024, Pezeshkian is scheduled to hold talks with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Iran's IRNA state news agency reported. The two-day BRICS Leaders' Summit begins on September 12 and is expected to bring together Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, among other leaders. Iran, which joined BRICS in 2024, is directly involved in the conflict, while fellow member the UAE has faced Iranian missile attacks and taken measures against Tehran. The UAE suspended all trade and financial transactions with Iran in August following the attacks, underscoring growing tensions within BRICS as the summit convenes amid the deepening regional crisis. The UAE is expected to be represented by Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan. With reporting by AFP and Reuters Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share 09:14 Oil Hits 4-Month High As Hormuz, Red Sea Risks Mount Oil prices surged to a four-month high on September 11 as escalating threats to two of the world's key energy shipping routes fueled fears of prolonged supply disruptions and renewed inflation. Brent crude touched $109.97 a barrel after jumping more than 6 percent a day earlier, before falling back. The benchmark was still on track for a weekly price gain of about 11 percent. Oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz remain restricted as the United States and Iran trade attacks, while the reported seizure of Yemen's Red Sea port of Mocha by Iran-aligned Houthi rebels has raised concerns over shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The oil rally intensified inflation concerns across global markets, pushing government bond yields sharply higher as investors increased bets on further interest-rate hikes. JPMorgan analysts now expect eight of nine developed-market central banks to raise interest rates by the end of the year as policymakers contend with persistent inflation and rising commodity prices. With reporting by Reuters Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share 08:18 Gulf States, Iran Plan Talks On Hormuz Shipping Deal, FT Reports Foreign ministers from Persian Gulf Arab states are expected to meet Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi in Oman next week as regional powers seek support for a temporary arrangement to restore commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the Financial Times reported . The meeting, an Omani initiative, is scheduled for September 14 in the coastal city of Salalah, according to two people briefed on the matter cited by the FT. One of the people said details were still being finalized, but that a number of states had confirmed their participation and the meeting was expected to go ahead. Oman and Iran have been negotiating a temporary arrangement under which ships would enter the strait through Iranian waters and mostly exit through Omani territory. Diplomats cautioned, however, that a US-Iran agreement would ultimately be needed for the waterway to fully reopen. One person briefed on the talks told the FT that Iran and Oman hoped to get GCC backing and use it to press Washington to lift its blockade of Iranian ports. Gulf states, meanwhile, want to ensure that any arrangement is temporary and allows vessels to enter and leave. The diplomatic push comes after a short-lived US-Iran memorandum of understanding signed in June unraveled amid disputes over shipping through Hormuz. body: Iran Anthropic Disrupts Iran’s Use Of Claude To Spread Propaganda, Spy On Dissidents By Frud Bezhan September 11, 2026 17:41 CET Anthropic Disrupts Iran’s Use Of Claude To Spread Propaganda, Spy On Dissidents Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Anthropic said it has disrupted attempts by Iran, China, and other countries from using its artificial intelligence (AI) models to disseminate state propaganda and spy on ethnic minorities and dissidents. That is according to the AI company’s latest threat intelligence report issued on September 11, which covers incidents from December 2025 to August. The report also said criminals, state institutions, and scientists, including in Russia and China, were using AI models like Claude and Gemini to design missiles and bombs as well as create deadly pathogens. SEE ALSO: Oil Hits 4-Month High As Hormuz, Red Sea Risks Mount 'Cognitive Warfare' Anthropic named several Iranian state institutions it said were using its AI models to shape public opinion inside and outside the country. The entities include the Islamic Culture and Communications Organization, which operates under the Ministry of Culture and Islamic Guidance and oversees Iran's official cultural diplomacy and international relations abroad; the Islamic Propaganda Office, a religious organization; and the Islamic Propaganda Organization, a religious and cultural group. Anthropic accused the institutions of running “cognitive warfare” campaigns and promoting narratives created by the powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, the elite branch of Iran’s armed forces that plays a prominent role in politics and the economy. “In each case, the operation relied on Claude to build campaign plans, doctrine manuals, persona systems, target databases, and ministerial planning documentation,” said Anthropic’s report. “Using the model in this manner allowed them to generate complex organizational frameworks and assets that would otherwise have required a fully staffed program office to produce.” In one case, the Islamic Culture and Communications Organization used Claude to “complete organizational plans” for the state funeral of slain Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei that took place from July 3-9, Anthropic said. SEE ALSO: From Russia With Expertise: Iranian Students Return Home With Potentially Deadly Knowledge Of Drones, AI, And More Recruitment Tool Anthropic also said it disrupted an “influence operation” by the Mujahedin-e Khalq (MEK), an exiled opposition group that seeks to overthrow the Islamic republic and that Tehran regards as a terrorist organization. The operation, the AI company said, “used a shared AI agent to impersonate real people and recruit inside Iran.” “The operation successfully scraped over 500 social media channels to build detailed profiles of individuals inside Iran,” the report said. “They then grouped these targets by city, age, occupation, political alignment, and arrest history likely to help them tailor their messages to the specific audiences.” Surveillance Operations Anthropic said it also disrupted operations by state actors, including Iran, that used Claude to “build, run, and otherwise facilitate surveillance operations.” In one case, Iran-based actors used Claude to build and deploy a malicious Firefox extension that harvested users’ identities from social media networks, the AI company said. In another case, an Iranian actor used Claude to analyze hundreds of thousands of social media posts and chose 39 opposition accounts to monitor. “The operators were state-aligned organizations that targeted the same diaspora and dissident communities these regimes have historically targeted,” Anthropic said. body: Iran 'Infiltration' Bill Exposes Iran's Internal Divisions Over Wartime Security Crackdown By Kian Sharifi September 10, 2026 15:43 CET 'Infiltration' Bill Exposes Iran's Internal Divisions Over Wartime Security Crackdown Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf speaks during an event marking 40 days since the burial of Iran's late Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, in Karbala, Iraq, on August 20. Iran's parliament is trying to turn fears of foreign infiltration into law. But as lawmakers work through the legislation, the debate is exposing an increasingly awkward question for the Islamic republic: How far should the state go in policing Iranians' contact with the outside world? At the center of that debate is Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, who, at least publicly, is doing a balancing act. He has defended the need for tougher measures against foreign infiltration while warning that the current draft of the legislation goes too far. "No patriot opposes countering foreign infiltration," Qalibaf said during a recent parliamentary session. But, he added, lawmakers needed to ensure that people's "rights, their lives, and their trade" were not affected. SEE ALSO: Iran Parliament Advances Bill Criminalizing Contact With Foreign Media and Institutions He said security agencies may need to be able to vet Iranians' contacts with foreigners but that they cannot demand permission at every stage. "They say they want to be certain, to have permission sought from them at every stage," the conservative speaker said. "That's not possible, because then we'd have to lock the country down." That balancing act gets to the heart of a bill that was conceived as a wartime response to genuine security failures. The two recent wars exposed how deeply Israeli intelligence had penetrated Iran and prompted calls for tougher measures to identify and prevent foreign influence. But what began as a security response has evolved into a much broader fight over the boundaries of the Islamic republic's security state. The bill, formally called the Plan To Counter The Infiltration Of Intelligence Services And Foreign Governments Or Institutions but commonly referred to as the "infiltration bill," would require Iranians to obtain prior approval from the Intelligence Ministry and the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) Intelligence Organization before engaging in a sweeping range of activities. Those activities include publishing books or articles, academic cooperation, interviews with foreign media deemed "hostile," and participation in scientific conferences or arts festivals. The bill also includes provisions criminalizing interviews, discussions, and other communication with media deemed hostile, as well as sending photographs, videos, audio, or other material to foreign media, with violations punishable by prison terms of up to two years. Parliament approved the bill's general framework in mid-August by a lopsided 183-4 vote. The draft has since expanded from 19 to 33 articles as it has moved through the National Security and Foreign Policy Committee. Only its first two articles have so far cleared the floor, while the remaining provisions remain subject to revision. Even if parliament approves them, the bill will still require Guardian Council approval before it can become law. The political resistance, however, has already begun. SEE ALSO: Oil Hits 4-Month High As Hormuz, Red Sea Risks Mount Qalibaf has sent two of the bill's most consequential provisions -- Articles 7 and 8, which deal with the disclosure process and penalties for exceeding the scope of a permit -- back to the committee because of ambiguities. Qalibaf has insisted that parliament must address the security agencies' concerns, saying their "needs" would be met "within reasonable bounds." But he has rejected the idea that the Intelligence Ministry and IRGC Intelligence Organization should effectively have the power to approve Iranians' foreign contacts at every turn. He has also dismissed suggestions that the bill should be shelved at the government's request. When First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref claimed Qalibaf had privately promised to stop the legislation, an MP repeated the allegation on the parliamentary floor. Qalibaf rejected it, stressing that parliament is not "a branch of the government." The result is a political fault line that does not fit neatly into Iran's usual hardliner-versus-reformist divide. Some lawmakers have been far more openly hostile to the bill. Mohammad Mehdi Shahriari, a member of the National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, called it "completely at odds with national interests." The government of President Masud Pezeshkian has also publicly opposed the bill. Hossein Afshin, the vice president for science, technology, and the knowledge-based economy, warned the current draft could isolate Iran's academic and research community and lead to "scientific stagnation." He pointed to the risks of an accelerated brain drain and additional obstacles for Iranian scientists working or studying abroad. Conservative commentator Mohammad Mohajeri, editor of Khabar Online, made much the same point more sarcastically, writing on X that just as the government was trying to persuade Iranians living abroad to return home, parliament was giving elites, scholars, and students fresh reasons to leave. The controversy has also attracted international criticism. On September 3, the UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran called for the bill to be withdrawn, warning it could further restrict fundamental freedoms and isolate Iranians from the international community. UN Special Rapporteur on Iran Mai Sato separately warned that Iranian intelligence agencies should not become "the gatekeepers of Iranian people's contact with the world." For Iran's political establishment, however, the more immediate problem may be closer to home. Few in the system appear willing to dispute that foreign infiltration is a genuine security threat. The argument is increasingly over what should follow from that threat and where the state should draw the line. body: © CABAR - Central Asian Bureau for Analytical Reporting Please make active links to the source, when using materials from this website На русском IWPR Kazakhstan is looking for an external M&E consultant to assess the impact and effectiveness of the Civil Society for Kazakhstan (CS4K) project through a final evaluation. About the project: The “Civil Society for Kazakhstan (CS4K)” project is funded by the European Union and being implemented by the Institute for War and Peace Reporting (IWPR) in Kazakhstan in partnership with the Public Foundation “Institute of National and International Development Initiatives” (INIDI). The project aims to promote fundamental freedoms and rights in Kazakhstan through the efforts of civil society. Specifically, the project is focused at building the capacity of local civil society organizations (CSOs) in advocacy and community engagement to promote changes, as well as sharing experiences between organizations. More information on the project can be found here: https://cs4k.cabar.asia/ The consultant(s) is expected to: Lead and coordinate final impact evaluation of the project, including designing evaluation framework, developing data collection tools, and conducting fieldwork, analysis and reporting. Design and manage data collection processes to ensure accuracy, reliability, and validity. Identify new verification sources for the project and, whenever possible, use existing data embedded in current systems. Study relevant project documents such as the work plan, event evaluation sheets, project content, log frame and result matrix, progress reports, and annual and mid-year evaluations. Revise the indicators (both target and achieved) accordingly. Engage with project stakeholders, including beneficiaries, partners, and donors, to gather input and feedback. Conduct qualitative and quantitative data analysis, comparing project progress against the established baseline. Outline trends of success, baseline-target vs. year achievements, and overall achievement. Evaluate the project’s short-term and long-term impact on target groups/individuals. Prepare and present comprehensive evaluation reports, providing actionable recommendations to improve project design, implementation, and impact. Uphold the values of freedom of speech, transparency, and accountability in all MEAL activities. Demonstrate a commitment to ethical evaluation practices and respect for participant confidentiality. Conduct debriefing and feedback sessions to support the utilization of findings with project staff, donors, partners, and others as per the previous agreement with the Project Manager. Scope of work: The overall objective of this evaluation is to provide the final review of the project by assessing its impact based on the OECD-DAC criteria, specifically focusing on effectiveness, impact and sustainability, efficiency, relevance and coherence. The final evaluation will aim to: Assess the project’s overall contribution to promoting fundamental freedoms and rights in Kazakhstan through civil society–led efforts, taking into account the broader political and social context. Examine the extent to which the project contributed to increased responsiveness of policy makers to civil society initiatives advancing human rights and democratic practices, including at local and national levels. Assess the project’s contribution to policy‐level influence, including civil society participation in the development or revision of government policies. Identify evidence of longer‐term or systemic changes in practices, attitudes, or relationships between civil society actors and decision‐makers that can be reasonably linked to the project. Draw lessons learned and strategic recommendations to strengthen the impact of future civil society support initiatives in similar contexts. A full terms of reference can be found here: https://iwprexternal.egnyte.com/dl/dyVHVgGVyH4Q Education: A minimum of a bachelor’s degree in international development, Human Rights, International Relations, Project Management, other Social Sciences or other related fields required. MA or other post-graduate capacities in relevant fields is desired. Skills and experience: Minimum 5 years of experience leading project evaluations. Strong expertise in Monitoring, Evaluation, and Learning (MEL), with proven experience in Outcomes Harvesting (leading, facilitating, and reporting). Demonstrated ability in qualitative analysis, mixed-method data management, and data visualization (e.g., graphs and dashboards). Highly organized and analytical, with adaptability and responsiveness to feedback and changing priorities. Ability to work effectively with minimal supervision, both independently and within small teams. Strong collaboration skills, with a flexible and efficient approach to work. Excellent virtual facilitation and written and spoken communication skills in English. Language: Advanced English and Russian; knowledge or understanding of the Kazakh language is desired. Travel: No travel is required for this position, however, willingness and ability to conduct in person KII/FGD is considered an advantage. Other requirements: Ability to work with colleagues remotely and to attend online (Zoom/Teams) meetings, storytelling sessions, etc. in GMT+5 time zone. How to Apply: Applicants interested in this call for application should apply at https://iwpr.bamboohr.com/careers/480 and submit the following documents to IWPR: A letter of interest outlining professional experience relevant to this consultancy. Short technical proposal (max. 5 pages) describing the methodology, tools, and techniques to deliver the evaluation, including capacity conduct in-person/remote interviews (including in Kazak), and any additional support needed (e.g., interpretation or workshop facilitation). Two evaluation reports from a previous project of a similar nature. Up-to-date CVs of the proposed consultants for this evaluation. Two (2) references from organisations for which the consultant or firm has carried out recent evaluations for similar projects (optional). Estimated overall budget broken down by categories including consultants’ working hours fee, translation/interpretation services, and other logistical needs. Note: The total budget must not exceed 7,000 EUR. Applications will be reviewed on a rolling basis, and IWPR reserves the right to fill the position before the closing date; early applications are therefore strongly encouraged, and interviews may be conducted prior to the deadline. IWPR will offer a competitive salary to the successful applicant. Principals only. No calls please. Only those who have been considered for an interview will be contacted.

body: © CABAR - Central Asian Bureau for Analytical Reporting Please make active links to the source, when using materials from this website На русском Қазақша From May to November 2025, IWPR and the Public Foundation “INIDI” held 10 practical workshops for recipients of funding for advocacy projects in the field of human rights as part of the “Civil Society for Kazakhstan” (CS4K) project, funded by the European Union. The workshops took place in eight cities of Kazakhstan: Almaty, Aktau, Kyzylorda, Pavlodar, Shymkent, Temirtau, Aktobe, and Astana. These events were part of comprehensive support for organizations that received funding under the project, aimed at strengthening their advocacy capacity, increasing the effectiveness of implemented initiatives, and promoting the formation of sustainable partnerships and coalitions. Topics and Approach Each workshop was focused on practical work with teams. Participants included funded organizations and their partner organizations, allowing work not only on the internal logic of campaigns but also on building inter-organizational cooperation. The program was designed to help teams develop practical, realistic, and structured campaigns based on their research and prepared policy briefs and white papers. What the participants did: Rechecked the logic of their policy briefs/white papers; Clarified advocacy goals and formulated expected outcomes; Conducted in-depth stakeholder analysis; Distributed roles within the coalition or team; Selected campaign strategies and tactics; Formulated key messages for different audiences; Created an action roadmap and content plan. Each team worked according to an adapted program considering the research topic, local context, and the specific needs of the organization. Workshop Results As a result of the workshops: 10 teams developed structured and realistic advocacy campaign plans; Roadmaps, stakeholder matrices, tactical plans, content plans, and message databases were created; Participants enhanced their understanding of coalition models and role distribution; Improved skills in strategic analysis, communication, and planning. Participants highly appreciated the practical focus, individual approach, and the opportunity to work with real documents. Many noted that the format helped to clarify campaign goals, identify potential risks, and form a more realistic action trajectory. “The workshop was held in a friendly atmosphere. Many questions were discussed in a short time, and the necessary materials were developed.” -Madina Tulepova, Public Foundation “Support of the Initiative” “It was excellent work with great results in a limited time. We are ready to continue improving our knowledge in organizing and conducting advocacy campaigns. Success and thanks for your contribution to the development of civil society.” -Maksim Kravchenko, Civil Alliance of Pavlodar Region “Overall, I really liked the training from the point of view of developing an advocacy strategy and identifying key players connected to the campaign results to varying degrees. I clearly saw the ‘white spots’ in our research and understood what additional recommendations could be included. Overall, it was a good opportunity to look at the advocacy plan from another perspective under the mentorship of an external specialist.” – Roman Reimer, Public Foundation “Wings of Liberty” The conducted workshops made an important contribution to strengthening civil society resilience and supporting local organizations implementing projects in the field of socially significant changes. Public Foundation “INIDI” and IWPR will continue to provide expert and methodological support to participants at all stages of implementing their initiatives. This publication was funded by the European Union. Its contents are the sole responsibility of IWPR and do not necessarily reflect the views of the European Union.
