body: Nouveau rapport RSF “Dans la peau d’un journaliste dans les Grands Lacs” : immersion dans le quotidien des reporters dans une région marquée par l’instabilité Crédit : Alexis Huguet / AFP Nouveau rapport RSF “Dans la peau d’un journaliste dans les Grands Lacs” : immersion dans le quotidien des reporters dans une région marquée par l’instabilité Organisation : RSF_fr RSF_Inter Partager facebook twitter linkedin Courriel Dans cette région teintée de rouge et d’orange sur la Carte mondiale de la liberté de la presse de Reporters sans frontières (RSF), les journalistes travaillent sous fortes pressions politiques et économiques. L’épicentre de la dégradation sécuritaire se situe dans l’est de la République démocratique du Congo (RDC), zone frontalière du Burundi, de l’Ouganda, de la Tanzanie et du Rwanda, où la circulation – contrainte ou non – de journalistes est constante. Au cœur des enjeux géopolitiques mondiaux liés aux ressources naturelles, la région des Grands Lacs est devenue un terrain particulièrement hostile à l’exercice du journalisme, entre violences, menaces et restrictions. Le nouveau rapport de RSF, “Dans la peau d’un journaliste des Grands Lacs”, plonge au cœur du quotidien de professionnels des médias qui informent malgré les risques. Lire en Swahili / Soma kwa Kiswahili Voir la carte en plein écran Lire le rapport ici Dans la peau d'un journaliste des Grands Lacs La liberté de la presse dans les six pays des Grands Lacs est soit “difficile” soit “très grave” : de la RDC (133e) au Kenya (102e), en passant par le Rwanda (146e), l’Ouganda (143e) le Burundi (125e) et la Tanzanie (95e), informer reste un défi quotidien. Dans son nouveau rapport, Dans la peau d’un journaliste dans les Grands Lacs , RSF révèle les violences multiformes auxquelles sont confrontés les professionnels des médias de la région. Car être “dans la peau d’un journaliste” dans cette région revient avant tout à exercer dans un environnement global dégradé. L’épicentre des difficultés sécuritaires se trouve dans l’est de la RDC, où le conflit a débuté à la fin des années 1990, quelques années après le génocide des Tutsi au Rwanda de 1994. Ces dernières années, et encore plus après la prise de la ville de Goma début 2025, informer de manière indépendante depuis l’est du pays est devenu presque impossible. Les reporters sont pris entre le marteau du groupe armé rebelle Mouvement du 23 mars (M23) et l’enclume des Forces armées de la RDC (FARDC). Conséquences : arrestations de journalistes, agressions, menaces, disparitions forcées, exécutions, médias suspendus, pillés ou saccagés... Les reporters n’ont souvent d’autre choix que de partir et de faire face aux défis du déplacement ou de l’exil, que ce soit vers la capitale de la RDC, Kinshasa, ou les pays voisins. Les difficultés dans la région ne se limitent pas aux zones de guerre : au Rwanda, l’environnement médiatique reste strictement contrôlé, poussant de nombreux journalistes à l’exil ; au Burundi, la presse reste fragilisée par les conséquences de la crise de 2015 ; en Ouganda, les reporters couvrant manifestations ou élections sont régulièrement confrontés à des arrestations et violences ; au Kenya, ils subissent des actes d’intimidation lorsqu’ils enquêtent sur la corruption ou les mobilisations sociales ; et en Tanzanie, les lois sur les médias continuent de restreindre fortement la liberté de la presse. À cela s’ajoutent des environnements juridiques et administratifs hostiles à la presse, une grande précarité économique et une forte perméabilité à la désinformation. “Les ennemis des journalistes ont plusieurs visages dans la région des Grands Lacs. Les reporters sont pris en étau entre violences armées, pressions politiques, asphyxie économique et désinformation, qui entravent durablement le droit des populations à une information fiable. Pour que cette dernière soit garantie, RSF appelle les États des Grands Lacs à agir sans délai et à protéger la sécurité des journalistes, à mettre fin à l’impunité des crimes commis contre eux et à garantir qu’ils puissent exercer leur métier sans craindre d’être incarcérés. Jeanne Lagarde Responsable plaidoyer du bureau de RSF pour l’Afrique subsaharienne Fruit du travail des équipes de RSF à Dakar, à Paris et dans la région des Grands Lacs, ce rapport se base sur le recueil de nombreux témoignages de journalistes et experts de la région, et sur un monitoring permanent de la situation de la liberté de la presse. Il pose également la question des moyens pour relever le défi d’informer, en mettant en lumière des initiatives de résilience et en formulant un certain nombre de recommandations. Les dix informations clés du rapport 1. Près de 500 journalistes arrêtés ou détenus depuis dix ans, la moitié en RDC Sur les dix dernières années, presque 500 journalistes ont été arrêtés dans la région des Grands Lacs en raison de leur travail, dont 111 ont été enfermés durant plus de deux jours. Parmi eux, Stanis Bujakera en RDC, Floriane Iraganbiye ou les journalistes de Iwacu au Burundi. Deux sont toujours détenus au Rwanda : Dieudonné Niyonsenga et Théoneste Nsengimana , alors qu’au Burundi, Sandra Muhoza est en liberté provisoire en attente de son verdict. 2. Des meurtres et disparitions en toute impunité Les cas des journalistes Jean Bigirimana , disparu au Burundi en 2016, Arshad Sharif , abattu par la police au Kenya en 2022, et John Williams Ntwali , tué dans un accident suspect au Rwanda en 2023, illustrent le niveau d’impunité et la gravité des menaces pesant sur la profession dans la région. Sur les dix dernières années, dix journalistes ont été tués et cinq ont disparu dans l’exercice de leur métier dans les Grands Lacs. 3. Un cadre juridique et administratif hostile Les six pays des Grands Lacs criminalisent les journalistes et leurs productions pour des charges aux contours flous et régulièrement utilisées de manière abusive, telles que “l’atteinte à l’intégrité du territoire national” ou “à la sûreté de l’État” et “l’insulte au chef de l’État” – à l’exception du Kenya pour cette dernière. La majorité d’entre eux criminalisent également la diffusion de fausses informations et la diffamation. Les suspensions de médias par les autorités de régulation – comme ceux du groupe Mwananchi Communications Limited en Tanzanie en 2024 pour un mois – et le contrôle administratif renforcé de la presse étrangère limitent la liberté d’informer dans la région : au Kenya, les accréditations coûtent quatre fois plus qu’il y a deux ans, soit environ 4 000 euros par an ; en Ouganda et en Tanzanie, elles coûtent plusieurs centaines d’euros. Les procédures sont longues, opaques, parfois arbitraires, et n’empêchent pas l’expulsion des journalistes. 4. Une précarité économique qui fragilise l’indépendance Avec des salaires très faibles et irréguliers – gravitant autour de 70 euros mensuels pour les journalistes de radios communautaires et entre 155 et 215 euros pour les journalistes de la région, avec de fortes disparités selon les médias et le statut – la plupart des journalistes doivent cumuler plusieurs activités pour survivre. Les médias manquent d’infrastructures et d’équipements essentiels et dépendent largement de financements publics et internationaux ou de revenus publicitaires, ce qui les rend vulnérables aux pressions. Au Kenya, longtemps considéré comme un pôle régional de liberté de la presse, l’indépendance des médias est fragilisée par des choix économiques, une tendance illustrée par le rachat controversé du groupe Nation Media Group par un homme d'affaires tanzanien jugé proche du président William Ruto en mars 2026. 5. La guerre à l’est de la RDC : épicentre du danger La RDC a enregistré le plus grand nombre de journalistes tués dans l’exercice de leur métier dans la région des Grands Lacs, soit cinq reporters tués depuis 2021 : Barthelemy Kubanabandu Changamuka ( CORAKI FM ), tué le 9 mai 2021, Héritier Magayane ( RTNC ), tué le 8 août 2021, Joël Musavuli ( RTCB ), tué le 14 août

body: Une année 2025 meurtrière pour les journalistes : voilà où mène la haine des journalistes, voilà où mène l’impunité Christina Atik / RSF Une année 2025 meurtrière pour les journalistes : voilà où mène la haine des journalistes, voilà où mène l’impunité 67 tués 503 détenus 135 disparus 20 otages Organisation : RSF_fr Partager facebook twitter linkedin Courriel Les journalistes ne meurent pas, ils sont tués. Le nombre de journalistes tués est reparti à la hausse, du fait des pratiques criminelles de forces armées régulières ou non et du crime organisé. Sur les 67 professionnels des médias tués durant l’année écoulée, ils sont ainsi au moins 53 à avoir été victimes de la guerre ou du crime organisé. Lire le bilan Bilan 2025 Lire en ukrainien / Читати українською Lire en russe / Читать на русском Près de la moitié (43 %) des journalistes tués ces 12 derniers mois l’ont été à Gaza , sous le feu des forces armées israéliennes. En Ukraine, l’armée russe continue elle aussi de cibler les reporters nationaux et internationaux. Quant au Soudan, il s’impose également comme un terrain de guerre particulièrement meurtrier pour la profession. Au Mexique, c’est le crime organisé qui est responsable d’une recrudescence alarmante des meurtres de journalistes en 2025. 2025 est l’année la plus meurtrière au Mexique depuis au moins trois an s et le pays est le deuxième plus dangereux pour les journalistes dans le monde, avec neuf journalistes tués. Et le phénomène s’étend avec une mexicanisation de l’Amérique latine : le continent américain concentre 24 % des journalistes tués dans le monde. Les journalistes nationaux paient le prix le plus élevé : seuls deux journalistes étrangers ont été tués hors de leur pays, le photoreporter français Antoni Lallican tué par une frappe de drone russe en Ukraine et le journaliste salvadorien Javier Hércules tué au Honduras, où il vivait depuis plus de dix ans. Tous les autres ont été tués en couvrant l’information dans leur pays. Mais outre la mort, ils sont la cible de bien d’autres exactions. 503 journalistes sont détenus à travers le monde : si la plus grande prison du monde est la Chine (121), la Russie (48) – qui a rejoint le trio de tête devant la Birmanie (47) – détient le plus grand nombre de journalistes étrangers : 26 Ukrainiens. En outre, un an après la chute de Bachar al-Assad, nombre de reporters arrêtés ou capturés sous son régime sont introuvables, faisant de la Syrie le pays comptant le plus – plus d’un quart du total – de professionnels des médias disparus dans le monde. “Voilà où mène la haine des journalistes ! Elle mène à la mort de 67 journalistes cette année, pas par accident, pas par effet collatéral. Ils ont été tués, ciblés en raison de leur activité de journaliste. La critique des médias est légitime et doit être force de changement pour garantir la survie de cette fonction sociale, mais sans jamais glisser dans la haine des journalistes, qui naît en grande partie, ou est entretenue, dans une volonté tactique de forces armées et de groupes criminels. Et voilà où mène l’impunité : l’échec des organisations internationales qui ne sont plus en mesure de faire respecter le droit sur la protection des journalistes en conflit armé est la conséquence d’un déclin du courage des gouvernements qui devraient déployer des politiques publiques de protection. De témoins privilégiés de l'histoire, les journalistes sont devenus progressivement des victimes collatérales, des témoins gênants, des monnaies d’échanges, des pions dans des jeux diplomatiques, des hommes et des femmes à abattre. Méfions-nous des facilités journalistiques : on ne donne pas sa vie pour le journalisme, on vous la vole ; les journalistes ne meurent pas, ils sont tués.” Thibaut Bruttin directeur général de RSF Regardez notre vidéo sur Youtube : 67 journalistes tués en 12 mois Depuis le 1er décembre 2024, 67 professionnels des médias ont été tués en raison de leur métier. Au moins 79% d’entre eux ont été victimes de forces armées régulières ou non – 37 journalistes – et du crime organisé – 16 journalistes. L’armée israélienne est responsable de plus de 43 % des crimes commis contre les journalistes sur les 12 derniers mois, soit près de la moitié d’entre eux. Au total, depuis octobre 2023, l’armée israélienne a tué près de 220 journalistes dont au moins 65 dans l’exercice ou en raison de leur travail. Alors qu’un an s’est écoulé depuis que Claudia Sheinbaum est devenue présidente du pays et malgré les engagements qu’elle a pris auprès de RSF, 2025 est l’année la plus meurtrière au Mexique depuis au moins trois ans et le pays est le deuxième plus dangereux pour les journalistes dans le monde, avec neuf journalistes tués. Les journalistes sont confrontés à de nombreuses exactions dans le cadre du conflit au Soudan. Quatre journalistes ont été tués dans l’exercice de leurs fonctions cette année, dont au moins deux après avoir été enlevés par les Forces de soutien rapide (FSR). Seuls deux journalistes tués sont des journalistes étrangers, tués hors de leur pays : le photoreporter français Antoni Lallican tué par une frappe de drone russe en Ukraine et le journaliste salvadorien Javier Hércules tué au Honduras, où il vivait depuis plus de dix ans. Tous les autres ont été assassinés en couvrant l’information dans leur pays. 503 journalistes sont emprisonnés dans le monde Au 1er décembre 2025, 503 journalistes sont détenus dans 47 pays du monde. La Chine (121) et la Birmanie (47) restent dans le trio de tête des plus grandes prisons de journalistes du monde et sont rejointes par la Russie (48), qui arrive à la deuxième place. Le pays de Vladimir Poutine est en outre celui qui détient le plus de journalistes étrangers au monde (26), suivi d’Israël (20). Au 1er décembre 2025, 113 professionnels des médias sont détenus par le régime de Xi Jinping, auxquels il faut ajouter huit autres journalistes à Hong-Kong. La République populaire de Chine reste la plus grande prison de journalistes du monde : elle en détient plus que la Russie et la Birmanie réunies. La situation en Russie, Géorgie, Azerbaïdjan ou encore au Bélarus, entre autres, illustre les graves dangers qui guettent la liberté de la presse dans les pays de l’ex-bloc soviétique. En Géorgie, l’implacable dérive autoritaire du gouvernement pro-russe a conduit à l’arrestation en janvier 2025 de la journaliste géorgienne Mzia Amaghlobeli. En Azerbaïdjan, 25 journalistes sont actuellement derrière les barreaux. Enfin, la Russie monte sur le deuxième marche du terrible podium des pays détenant le plus de journalistes : 48 au premier décembre 2025, dont 26 Ukrainiens. Israël est le second pays après la Russie à emprisonner le plus de journalistes étrangers. Au premier décembre 2025, 20 journalistes palestiniens se trouvent encore dans les geôles israéliennes. Parmi eux, 16 ont été arrêtés au cours des deux dernières années à Gaza et en Cisjordanie. 72 % des journalistes disparus au Moyen-Orient et en Amérique Latine En 2025, 135 journalistes sont toujours portés disparus, dans 37 pays du monde. Certains depuis plus de 30 ans. Si aucun continent n’est épargné, ce phénomène se manifeste particulièrement au Mexique (28) et en Syrie (37). 37 journalistes sont aujourd’hui portés disparus en Syrie. Pour beaucoup, ils étaient otages de L’État islamique ou prisonniers de Bachar al-Assad, mais leur chute n’a pas encore permis de les retrouver. 72 % des journalistes actuellement introuvables ont disparu dans des pays du Moyen-Orient ou d’Amérique latine, essentiellement en Syrie, en Irak et au Mexique Vingt journalistes otages dans le monde Vingt journalistes sont toujours retenus en otage dans le monde. En 2025, les rebelles houthis ont pris en otage sept nouveaux journalistes, faisant du Yémen le pays où le plus de journalistes ont subi ce type d’enlèvement ces 12 derniers mois. body: La liberté de la presse sous pression en Allemagne en raison de la désinformation, de la polarisation politique et des attaques contre le journalisme Organisation : RSF_fr Partager facebook twitter linkedin Courriel Les journalistes en Allemagne sont confrontés à des menaces croissantes alors que la polarisation politique, la désinformation et l'hostilité envers les médias continuent de s'intensifier. Le rapport “Focus 2026” de Reporters sans frontières (RSF) sur la situation de la liberté de la presse en Allemagne met en lumière la fragilité croissante, marquée par des agressions physiques, du harcèlement en ligne, des pressions politiques et des réponses politiques insuffisantes tant au niveau national qu'européen. De nombreux reporters en Allemagne perçoivent la délégitimation du travail journalistique comme une menace majeure pour le journalisme dans leur pays, comme le montre le rapport récemment publié “ Focus 2026 : Rapport de RSF sur l'état de la liberté de la presse en Allemagne ” ( “Nahaufnahme 2026 : RSF-Report zur Lage der Pressefreiheit in Deutschland” ). Cette tendance est alimentée par les acteurs politiques, le harcèlement numérique et les nouveaux formats médiatiques qui donnent naissance à des médias peu fiables qui gagnent en audience grâce à la polarisation et à la désinformation. Depuis des années, cette polarisation et un climat social difficile ont également entraîné des risques pour la sécurité : RSF Allemagne a documenté et vérifié un total de 55 agressions en 2025 contre des professionnels des médias et des rédactions. En 2024, 89 incidents avaient été recensés. Comme les années précédentes, la couverture des manifestations et des groupes d'extrême droite s'est avérée particulièrement dangereuse. Des attaques isolées ont également été signalées de la part d'acteurs d'extrême gauche et des forces de sécurité. La couverture du Moyen-Orient divise les professionnels des médias et la société civile Les rédactions ont continué à connaître un climat tendu autour de la couverture de la Palestine et d'Israël. En 2025, les journalistes ont une fois de plus rencontré des difficultés pour couvrir les violations des droits humains commises par l'armée israélienne. Dans le cadre de la couverture de la guerre à Gaza, le paysage médiatique est devenu de plus en plus fragmenté. Alors que certains journalistes, qui critiquaient légitimement les violations commises par le gouvernement israélien à Gaza, ont été calomniés, exposés et discrédités comme antisémites, d'autres journalistes couvrant le conflit du côté israélien ont également été la cible de campagnes de haine antisémites et de diffamation, pour avoir fait leur travail. Insécurité en exil : répression transnationale Les journalistes exilés vivant en Allemagne sont par ailleurs régulièrement pris pour cible par leurs autoritaires États d'origine. Les gouvernements tentent de les intimider en menaçant de recourir à la violence contre les journalistes ou leurs familles. Ils sont également espionnés et empêchés de faire leur travail. Pour les journalistes afghans, russes et iraniens, les conditions dans leur pays d'origine sont, dans certains cas, dangereuses pour leur vie, ce qui est exacerbé par la suspension des programmes d'admission humanitaire pour ces pays et le non-respect par le gouvernement allemand de ses promesses de protéger ou de relocaliser ces reporters. Le pouvoir des géants de la technologie Les politiques du second mandat de Donald Trump ont également influencé le discours public et le paysage médiatique en Allemagne. Les grandes entreprises technologiques laissent la polarisation politique s'épanouir sur leurs plateformes de réseaux sociaux, et l'administration Trump soutient leur résistance aux réglementations de l'Union européenne (UE). Leurs algorithmes favorisent la désinformation, leurs plateformes facilitent les campagnes de désinformation en provenance de Russie et la vérification des faits intégrée aux plateformes a été supprimée. Ces grandes plateformes technologiques permettent aux discours haineux et aux tentatives politiques visant à détourner la couverture médiatique de sujets importants et controversés d'atteindre une audience considérable. La législation allemande et européenne répond à cela par une inaction persistante. Cela aggrave les divisions sociales et contribue à monter délibérément les citoyens allemands les uns contre les autres. “Le journalisme, la politique et la société civile ne doivent pas céder face aux multiples défis technologiques posés par ceux qui cherchent à vider le secteur de l'information de sa substance au profit du pouvoir et des intérêts économiques” , déclare Katharina Viktoria Weiß, référente Allemagne de RSF et co-auteure du rapport précité. Surveillance et politique médiatique en Allemagne et au niveau de l'UE Au niveau de l'UE, l'attaque contre les communications cryptées de bout en bout par le biais d'un contrôle indiscriminé des messageries a été temporairement évitée. Cependant, l'utilisation de “chevaux de Troie gouvernementaux” par le Service fédéral de renseignement (BND) reste une préoccupation majeure. RSF a déposé une plainte à ce sujet auprès de la Cour européenne des droits de l'homme (CEDH). La directive européenne contre les poursuites judiciaires stratégiques visant à entraver la participation publique (SLAPP), autrement dit les procédures-baillons, doit encore être transposée en Allemagne ; le projet actuel du gouvernement n'offre que peu de protection concrète aux professionnels des médias menacés. Dans l'ensemble, la politique médiatique allemande n'a guère progressé vers le renforcement du journalisme et de la diversité des médias. Contrairement à ce qui était prévu dans l'accord de coalition, il n'existe toujours pas de projet d'incitations fiscales pour le journalisme à but non lucratif. L'augmentation – attendue depuis longtemps – de la redevance audiovisuelle continue d'être bloquée par les Länder. Seul le traité réformant l'audiovisuel public, entré en vigueur le 1er décembre 2025, a été ratifié par tous les Länder après de longues négociations. Publié le 06.02.2026 Europe - Asie centrale Allemagne Désinformation et propagande Violences contre les journalistes Rapport Plateformes Technologies Agressions Cyberharcèlement

body: Press release OSCE Economic and Environmental Forum focuses on anticipating technologies and science diplomacy for emerging security risks Date: 10 September 2026 Place: PRAGUE Source: OSCE Chairpersonship , OSCE Secretariat PRAGUE, 10 September 2026 – The OSCE today opened its 32nd Economic and Environmental Forum (EEF) in Prague, focusing on how anticipating technological developments and strengthening science-based diplomacy can contribute to security and stability across the OSCE area by helping participating States better prepare for both existing and emerging challenges. Organized by the Office of the Co-ordinator of OSCE Economic and Environmental Activities under the guidance of Switzerland’s 2026 OSCE Chairpersonship, the two-day conference brings together representatives of OSCE participating States, Partners for Co-operation, international organizations, academia, the private sector and civil society. Participants are examining how the OSCE can strengthen its ability to anticipate technological developments, assess their implications for security and stability, and better prepare for a rapidly changing economic and environmental landscape. The discussion follows a Joint Preparatory Meeting of the EEF in Vienna from 7 and 8 September under the same title. In his address to the EEF participants, OSCE Chairman-in-Office, Swiss Federal Councillor Ignazio Cassis, recalled that “Anticipation is a political necessity. This is why Switzerland has chosen Anticipating technologies as a priority of its Chairpersonship. We must anchor this approach in the OSCE, because technology already affects all three dimensions of the OSCE.” As host of the event, which is taking place at Czernin Palace, Czech Deputy Prime Minister Petr Macinka, opened the EEF: “We must prepare the OSCE for the security challenges of tomorrow,” Minister Macinka said in his opening remarks. He stressed that new technologies, including artificial intelligence and quantum technologies, can become major sources of prosperity, innovation and resilience, while also creating new risks and changing the nature of security threats. “If we want to prevent conflicts and misunderstandings, we need to understand the impact of technological change before it catches us by surprise. This is precisely where the OSCE can play an important role,” the Czech Foreign Minister added. “Today, as geopolitical fragmentation is growing, we are also at the dawn of a new technological revolution. The direction this transformation takes will depend on the choices we make – collectively, as governments, as societies and as the international community. No single country, company, or institution can make those choices alone. This is why we need dialogue, co-operation and science-based diplomacy. And this is why our ability to anticipate matters so much,” said OSCE Secretary General Feridun H. Sinirlioğlu. During the opening session, the State Secretary of the Swiss Federal Department of Foreign Affairs, Alexandre Fasel, stated that “The OSCE was founded on a comprehensive approach to security. This common ground endures despite our current divisions: the fact that we were able to agree to hold this Forum is a clear demonstration of this.” The Forum offers concrete follow-up to one of Switzerland’s priorities for its 2026 Chairpersonship: “anticipating technologies – for a safe and humane future”. It builds in particular on the international conference hosted in Geneva on 7and 8 May, which brought together experts from science, technology, diplomacy and policymaking to examine how anticipation can help societies prepare for rapid technological change. In Prague, participants are discussing how the OSCE can make better use of technological and scientific expertise in decision-making, strengthen anticipatory capacities and preparedness, and develop effective approaches to new technologies, including in relation to economic and environmental issues, in particular water, energy and economic good governance. The focus of this mandated, second dimension conference is part of the Swiss Chairpersonship’s broader effort to strengthen the OSCE’s ability to act in a changing security environment. For more information about this year’s event, click here . body: Press release Dialogue and education are key to prevent violence based on religion or belief, OSCE human rights body says Date: 21 August 2026 Place: WARSAW Source: OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights WARSAW, 21 August 2026 – Education about religions and beliefs, together with interfaith and interreligious dialogue, can help counter prejudice and hostility that can lead to violence, the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR) said in a statement ahead of tomorrow’s International Day Commemorating the Victims of Acts of Violence Based on Religion or Belief. “Across the OSCE region, individuals and communities continue to face violence on account of their religion or belief, and states have a duty to prevent and effectively respond to such violence,” said ODIHR Director Maria Telalian. “They can do this by creating the conditions for mutual respect and peaceful coexistence, including through education that instills respect for the human dignity of each person, strengthening resilience to polarizing narratives, and equipping people to recognize and respond to misinformation and disinformation.” “Dialogue across religious and belief boundaries can help make diversity a familiar part of everyday life, encouraging understanding instead of fear, and helping to prevent and counter prejudice,” she said. Year after year, ODIHR’s annual Hate Crime Report documents that individuals and communities are targeted on the basis of religion or belief across broad sectors of society and in a range of spaces, including online. Limited opportunities for people to meet and understand those they perceive as different can allow stereotypes and prejudice to take hold. In the absence of direct interaction, perceptions can, instead, be shaped by hearsay, prejudice, misinformation and disinformation that exploit and reinforce fears that can fuel hostility. Online platforms can further amplify the spread of divisive or misleading content. “Respect for human rights, including freedom of religion or belief, means recognizing that people have the right to hold and express different religious or non-religious convictions, including the belief that their own religion or worldview is true, while respecting the rights and dignity of those who believe differently,” the ODIHR Director said. Through their OSCE commitments, participating States have committed to promote interfaith and intercultural dialogue as a way to foster respect and mutual understanding, and to counter intolerance. They have also undertaken to address the root causes of intolerance and discrimination through education. ODIHR assists in this work by providing guidance on fostering dialogue, as well as practical tools, resources and capacity-building support on freedom of religion or belief and hate crimes for state officials and civil society actors. body: News News Item Public broadcasters must not amplify the glorification of convicted war criminals Issued on: 7 September 2026 Issued by: OSCE Mission to Bosnia and Herzegovina , OSCE Representative on Freedom of the Media Fields of work: Human rights , Rule of law SARAJEVO/VIENNA, 07 September 2026 - The OSCE Mission to Bosnia and Herzegovina and the OSCE Representative on Freedom of the Media express serious concern regarding RTRS’s direct live transmission of a commemoration at which speakers repeatedly glorified Ratko Mladić. His convictions for genocide, crimes against humanity and violations of the laws or customs of war were upheld on appeal in 2021, as was his sentence of life imprisonment. Reporting on events of legitimate public interest is an essential part of media freedom and editorial independence. While reporting on events of public interest falls within the media’s editorial remit, particular concern arises given that content glorifying a convicted war criminal was amplified without adequate editorial context or reference to judicially established facts. Public service broadcasters have a particular responsibility to provide accurate, impartial and properly contextualized journalism. The Mission recalls that Article 145a(6) of the Criminal Code of Bosnia and Herzegovina criminalizes the glorification of persons sentenced by final judgment for such crimes. Whether the broadcast may have breached criminal law is for the competent justice institutions to determine. Separately, the Mission and the Representative call on the Communications Regulatory Agency to assess the coverage promptly and independently, including under Articles 4(8), 5 and 7 of the CRA Code on Programme Content, and to respond proportionately to any violation established. Respect for judicially established facts and for the dignity of victims and survivors is fundamental to responsible journalism, reconciliation and lasting peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Any media coverage of the forthcoming funeral should accordingly be accurate, properly contextualized and consistent with applicable professional and ethical standards. body: News News Item OSCE calls for safeguarding BHRT’s independence and functioning ahead of elections Issued on: 6 September 2026 Issued by: OSCE Mission to Bosnia and Herzegovina Fields of work: Media freedom and development SARAJEVO, 06 September 2026 - The OSCE Mission to Bosnia and Herzegovina (Mission) calls on all relevant authorities to respect and implement binding court decisions, safeguard judicial independence and ensure the functioning and independence of BHRT ahead of the elections. Public service broadcasters play a particularly important role during elections by providing citizens with reliable information needed to make informed decisions. Beyond the immediate measures needed to ensure BHRT’s continued functioning, a sustainable long-term framework for public service broadcasting is necessary, with strong safeguards for its independence. The Mission also calls on all public officials, candidates and political parties to respect media freedom and provide an enabling environment for journalists to work freely and independently during the election period. body: News News Item Electoral Integrity and Public Confidence at the Heart of the 2026 General Elections Issued on: 3 September 2026 Issued by: OSCE Mission to Bosnia and Herzegovina Fields of work: Elections SARAJEVO, 3 September 2026 – With Bosnia and Herzegovina’s 2026 General Elections approaching, the OSCE Mission to Bosnia and Herzegovina and Civil Society BiH today brought together election officials, civil society, media, academia and international partners to discuss new election technologies, electoral integrity and the importance of a peaceful and democratic election campaign. The conference , “What Can We Expect from the 2026 Elections? New Electoral Technologies, Election Integrity, and a Democratic Election Campaign,” takes place one day before the official campaign begins and one month ahead of Election Day on 4 October. For the first time, the General Elections will involve biometric voter identification and authentication, as well as ballot scanners and electronic transmission of election results. The Mission has worked closely with the Central Election Commission of Bosnia and Herzegovina (CEC BiH) in supporting preparations for the introduction of these technologies, alongside its broader support for electoral integrity and voter education. “These new technologies will make the electoral process more accurate, transparent and efficient, but it is not just technology alone that builds public confidence in election results,” said Ambassador Rick Holtzapple, Head of the OSCE Mission to Bosnia and Herzegovina. “Confidence also depends on how elections are administered, observed, reported and explained to voters. All those involved, institutions, political parties, observers, civil society and the media, have a responsibility to contribute to an electoral process that citizens can trust.” "Despite strong support from international organizations and individual global powers for electoral integrity, democratic campaigning, and the building of a democratic society, and, to a certain extent, the introduction of new technologies, the responsibility for the integrity of the electoral process lies primarily with the politicians. They must demonstrate whether they are all finally committed to progress, democracy, and the European path, or if some still wish to continue with the undemocratic and corrupt practices of the past," said Laura Bošnjak, Project Manager of Civil Society BiH. "It is the citizens who elect them; therefore, those citizens must recognize serious platforms, turn out to vote in the largest possible numbers, and decide to whom they will entrust their future and what that future will look like. Participants also discussed the responsibility of political parties to conduct a peaceful, constructive and substantive campaign focused on issues affecting citizens, rather than divisive rhetoric and narratives that heighten ethno-national tensions. Particular attention was given to the participation of first-time voters and to the importance of accurate voter information about the new voting procedures. The OSCE Mission to BiH and Civil Society BiH call on all eligible citizens to exercise their right to vote on 4 October 2026, to seek information from reliable sources and to reject divisive rhetoric and misinformation. They also call on political parties and candidates to offer voters a peaceful, issue-based campaign focused on concrete solutions and the future of all citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina. body: 02/09/2026 Report Thailand en fr th VALERIA MONGELLI / ANADOLU / ANADOLU VIA AFP A new report published by the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) and its member organisation Thai Lawyers for Human Rights (TLHR) sheds light on the severe human rights impacts of the enforcement of Article 112 of Thailand’s Criminal Code (lèse-majesté) since the country’s latest military coup in May 2014. Bangkok, Paris, 2 September 2026. The report, titled " The unsayable - Q&A on Thailand’s lèse-majesté" , answers 15 frequently asked questions about Article 112 and its implications for human rights, civic space, the media, and democratic development in Thailand. " The evidence of the serious human rights violation linked to the enforcement of Article 112 is overwhelming and causes great damage to Thailand’s international standing. Reform of Article 112 is long overdue and efforts by Thai civil society to peacefully campaign for such changes should be commended and protected, " said FIDH Vice-President Teppei Ono. Statistics about lèse-majesté reflect the severity and scope of the human rights violations linked to the enforcement of Article 112. Between May 2014 and July 2026, at least 461 individuals were prosecuted under Article 112, with at least 199 receiving prison sentences. The 10 longest prison sentences imposed under Article 112 averaged approximately 30 years and six months, with the longest sentence reaching 50 years. At least 21 children were prosecuted under Article 112, with the youngest one aged 14. As of July 2026, 29 individuals remained detained under Article 112. Of these, 12 were detained pending trial or appeal, while the judgments for the remaining 17 had become final. Among those behind bars is prominent pro-democracy activist and human rights lawyer Arnon Nampa, who has accumulated a prison term of over 31 years stemming from 11 lèse-majesté convictions for his speeches and online posts that called for monarchy reform. Three additional lèse-majesté cases remain pending. At the international level, all the relevant key United Nations (UN) human rights mechanisms have consistently expressed their concerns over various aspects of the enforcement of Article 112 and declared it incompatible with Thailand’s human rights obligations under international law. Many states also expressed growing concern over the issue of lèse-majesté during Thailand’s Universal Periodic Review (UPR). Thailand’s fourth UPR is scheduled for 9 November 2026. FIDH and TLHR call on states to use Thailand’s fourth UPR to raise their concerns over the ongoing abuse of Article 112 and make recommendations to the Thai government to bring this provision into line with international law. FIDH and TLHR also urge Thai authorities to establish a moratorium on new lèse-majesté prosecutions and to immediately release all those who are being deprived of their liberty under Article 112. body: 31/08/2026 Press release Democratic Republic of Congo en es fr Belgium Corruption NICOLAS MAETERLINCK / BELGA MAG / BELGA VIA AFP For the first time, a Belgian company will have to answer in court over allegations that it bribed foreign public officials. Congolese citizens, supported by a coalition of organisations, have joined the proceedings as civil parties before the Belgian courts. Part of the money paid for passports has allegedly been channelled to a relative of former Congolese President Joseph Kabila. The civil parties hope that justice will now be served in this case, which has been ongoing for nine years, and concerns the alleged embezzlement of US$60 million. Kinshasa, Brussels, 31 August 2026. The civil parties welcome the decision handed down this morning by the Brussels Council Chamber today to refer the 14 defendants in the Semlex case to the criminal court. They will have to answer allegations of bribery of foreign public officials, money laundering and tax fraud in connection with the contract for Congolese biometric passports. Semlex, the company that produced the Democratic Republic of Congo’s (DRC) biometric passports between 2015 and 2025, is the first Belgian company to be referred to a Belgian criminal court over alleged foreign bribery, with the prospect of the case being examined on its merits. In May 2020, 51 Congolese citizens brought a civil action before the Belgian courts with the support of the coalition Le Congo n’est pas à vendre (Congo Is Not For Sale). They were joined by the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH), the Human Rights League (LDH), UNIS, Transparency International and Transparency International Belgium, all of which joined the proceedings as civil parties in this landmark case. The civil parties commend the work of the investigators who, over nearly nine years, traced bank transactions, analysed hundreds of emails and electronic messages, interviewed numerous witnesses and suspects, and carried out letters rogatory in the DRC and the United Arab Emirates, where several of the companies involved were registered. This is one of the most thorough investigations ever conducted in Belgium into allegations of international corruption. A US$60 million case The accused are alleged to have set up a large-scale corruption scheme centred on the biometric passport contract. According to documents reported in the press, for every passport sold for US$185, US$60 was allegedly channeled to LRPS Ltd, a Dubai-based company believed to be linked to a close associate of former DRC President Joseph Kabila. The scheme is alleged to have resulted in the diversion of nearly US$60 million. For the civil parties, this case concerns, above all, the Congolese people. " We paid $185 for our passports, before learning from the press that some of that money had allegedly been used to bribe members of the political elite. We have a right to know where our money went. This trial will finally shed light on the matter " said Fred Bauma, Congolese citizen acting as a civil claimant . " It is hoped that this case will also shed light on responsibilities at the Congolese level, which could lead to further legal action in the DRC, so that all those responsible in this case are held to account for their actions before the competent courts ", said Jean-Claude Katende, Vice-President of the FIDH and President of the African Association for the Defence of Human Rights (ASADHO) . This decision also marks a significant step forward for the Belgian justice system. Despite its commitments under the OECD Anti-Bribery Convention and the United Nations Convention against Corruption , the country has been criticised on several occasions for its inadequate enforcement of laws against the bribery of foreign public officials. This trial will be a major test of its ability to uphold these commitments. " For far too long, Belgium has fallen short of its commitments to combat international corruption. This referral to court is historic: it demonstrates that a Belgian company can be held to account for serious alleged acts of corruption committed abroad " said Transparency International Belgium . The signatory organisations stress that those brought before the court are presumed innocent. They hope that the trial will establish responsibility and send a clear message: Belgian companies must be held to account for their actions, including when alleged acts of corruption are committed abroad. body: 12/08/2026 Statement Chad en es fr International Criminal Court (ICC) JORIS BOLOMEY / AFP The announcement by Chadian authorities of their decision to withdraw from the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (ICC) marks a worrying setback for the fight against impunity for the most serious crimes and for victims’ rights. Chad’s commitment to international justice is called into question at a time when the international justice system is facing growing attacks and when state cooperation is more essential than ever. N’Djamena, 12 August 2026. On 27 July 2026, the Government of the Republic of Chad decided to withdraw from the Rome Statute of the ICC. The International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH), the Chadian League for Human Rights (LTDH), the Chadian Association for the Promotion and Defense of Human Rights (ATPDH), and the Public Interest Law Center (PILC) express their profound indignation and condemn this decision. The Rome Statute does not replace national courts; it operates on the basis of complementarity, stepping in when national courts lack the capacity or willingness to investigate and prosecute the most serious crimes. Withdrawal does not strengthen the ability of national courts to deliver justice; instead, it deprives victims of an alternative path to obtaining it. Chad’s withdrawal represents a further setback for the global fight against impunity and for victims’ rights, at a time when the Court is facing unprecedented attacks, including the U.S. government’s campaign to dismantle the ICC . Chad’s announcement does not, however, carry immediate legal consequences. Article 127 of the Rome Statute governs the effects of such a withdrawal: it takes effect only one year after written notification to the UN Secretary-General , in this case, on 27 July 2027. Moreover, withdrawal does not release the State concerned from obligations incurred while it was a party to the Statute, including the obligation to cooperate with the Court on investigations and criminal proceedings already underway before the withdrawal takes effect, and it does not affect investigations or proceedings the Court had already opened before that date. Chad’s withdrawal, should it go forward, therefore cannot erase the past or prevent the Court from exercising jurisdiction over crimes committed before it takes effect. Chad’s announcement comes amid a growing challenge to international criminal justice and the ICC. The three member States of the Alliance of Sahel States (Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger) also recently announced their withdrawal from the ICC. Those withdrawals will take effect on 18 June 2027 for Niger, and 24 June 2027 for Burkina Faso and Mali. African States nonetheless played an essential role in the creation of the Court in 1998, ratifying the Rome Statute in large numbers and even referring certain domestic situations to the Court’s jurisdiction. That commitment gave victims of the most serious crimes an international ally when justice could not be obtained at the national level. Chad’s announced withdrawal runs counter to this history of African leadership, leaving victims with fewer means of obtaining justice. While the ICC has in the past been criticised for the selectivity of the cases it opens and for what was seen as excessive focus on Africa, the Court has progressively worked to strengthen the universality of its mandate, extending its work well beyond the African continent, with ongoing investigations and cases in Afghanistan, Bangladesh/Myanmar, Palestine, Ukraine, Venezuela, and the Philippines. The recent arrest of former President Rodrigo Duterte demonstrated that no region and no senior official is beyond the reach of justice. This universality strengthens the Court’s legitimacy but also makes it more vulnerable to political attacks. The organisations call on Chadian authorities to reverse their decision to withdraw from the ICC and to reaffirm their commitment to the Rome Statute and to international justice. As Chad hosts several hundred thousand refugees from Darfur, many of whom have suffered serious violations of international humanitarian and human rights law, this announcement sends an alarming signal to victims. Victims of the most serious international crimes must not be the first casualties of States’ political choices. When national courts are unable or unwilling to deliver justice, the ICC remains an essential mechanism of last resort to guarantee victims’ right to truth, justice, and reparation. At a time when serious human rights violations persist in many parts of the world, States should be strengthening international mechanisms against impunity, not distancing themselves from them. FIDH, LTDH, ATPDH, and PILC reaffirm their determination to continue, alongside the whole of Chadian and international civil society, the fight against impunity and for justice, victims’ dignity, and respect for human rights in Chad. body: 10/09/2026 Report Ecuador en es fr Human Rights Defenders Antonella Calle International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) and six international organisations denounce the climate of repression and militarisation in Ecuador. A new report, prepared following a visit to Ecuador, includes on-the-ground interviews with various communities, human rights defenders, local authorities, and representatives of the international community. Quito, September 10, 2026. Following an observation visit conducted in March 2026, the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) and the World Organisation Against Torture (OMCT), within the framework of the Observatory for the Protection of Human Rights Defenders, Front Line Defenders (FLD), CIVICUS: Global Alliance for Citizen Participation, 11.11.11 – Coalition for International Solidarity, the Association of Human Rights Lawyers, Judges, and Prosecutors of Latin America and the Caribbean (Asociación de Abogadas, Abogados, Jueces y Fiscales de Derechos Humanos de América Latina y el Caribe – AJUFIDH), Peace Brigades International (PBI), and the World Rainforest Movement (WRM) are publishing a joint report today that warns of the rapid deterioration of the human rights and environmental situation in Ecuador. Against a backdrop marked by the militarisation of public security, the weakening of the rule of law, and a growing link between extractive conflicts and the securitisation of territories, the report, in spanish only, " Ataques y criminalización contra la sociedad civil en un contexto de militarización y extractivismo en Ecuador " presents the following findings. Setback in the Rule of Law Since March 2024, the government has repeatedly imposed states of emergency, declared internal armed conflict, and expanded the role of the Armed Forces in public safety, thereby normalising exceptional measures that have failed to reduce public insecurity in the country. On the contrary, the number of violent deaths has reached historic highs, and serious human rights violations are being reported in militarized areas, with disproportionate impacts on Indigenous peoples, Afrodescendant communities, and rural campesino communities. " Ecuador stands at a crossroads: either it strengthens the rule of law or it deepens the crisis. Exceptional measures cannot become the new normal, and socioenvironmental conflicts cannot be resolved through the militarisation of territories. A security policy in the country must address the multidimensional causes of violence and must adhere to international law, " states Soraya Gutierrez, Secretary General of the FIDH. Institutional Weakening The organisations note attacks on the Constitutional Court, challenges to judicial independence, delays in the administration of justice, and in the enforcement of court rulings, as well as an insufficient response from the Defensoría del Pueblo (Ombudsman’s Office / People’s Advocate Office) to the criminalisation and freezing of bank accounts of human rights defenders and civil society organisations. In this regard, César Sivo, president of AJUFIDH , states that " judicial independence is non-negotiable: without autonomous powers, the rule of law vanishes and justice becomes a mirage ". Criminalisation of Protest and Shrinking of Civic Space The report identifies patterns of violent repression against peaceful protests led by Indigenous movements, including criminalisation, stigmatisation, and the persecutory use of administrative, financial, and legal measures against human rights defenders and civil society organisations. " We observed a concerning and accelerating deterioration of civic space. The violent repression of the 2025 national strike, coupled with the increase in threats and attacks against journalists, as well as regulatory obstacles to the operation of civil society organisations, create an increasingly hostile environment for the exercise of civic freedoms, " emphasised Eduardo Marenco, Advocacy Officer for the Americas at CIVICUS. Attacks on Human Rights and Environmental Defenders, Civil Society Organisations and Social Movements The visit documents an alarming rate of violence and attacks against human rights and environmental defenders and civil society organisations, with particular attention to cases of criminalization, while the State fails to acknowledge the scale of this problem and adopt robust and effective measures to prevent these violations and protect defenders. " Defending human rights and nature is not a crime, as Ecuador’s own Constitution recognises. The criminalisation, stigmatisation, and attacks against defenders in Ecuador must cease immediately. The State has an obligation to protect those who defend the rights of their communities, not to persecute them, " says Álvaro Gómez del Valle, Advocacy Lead for the Americas at Front Line Defenders. The Rise of Extractivism Far from being a mere sectoral economic policy, extractivism—which spans the mining, oil, agro-industrial, fishing, and hydroelectric sectors—emerges as a web of regulatory, institutional, and security decisions that favor its expansion in the name of economic growth and investment stability in the country. This dynamic occurs at the expense of guarantees of participation, protection of rights, and compliance with democratic and judicial decisions, without respecting Ecuador’s international human rights obligations, which ultimately affect community governance, livelihoods, and the ability of communities to make free and informed decisions regarding their own territories. Regarding this serious issue, Carla Moscoso, Coordinator for the Andean Region of 11.11.11 , notes that " What is at stake is who decides on the territories, which ways of life are protected, and who bears the social and environmental costs of the conflicts, in the face of certain perspectives or categories such as ‘national interest,’ ‘strategic security,’ or ‘strategic sectors’ ." Among their urgent recommendations, the organisations urge the Ecuadorian government to: – align security policies with the principles of legality, necessity, and proportionality, with civilian and judicial oversight over the use of force; – guarantee the independence of public authorities; – put an end to the stigmatisation and criminalisation of protesters, individuals, and organisations defending human and nature rights; – protect human rights and nature defenders and groups through comprehensive policies that incorporate a gender and intercultural perspective; – respect the free, prior, and informed consent of communities affected by extractive projects. At the same time, the organisations call on the international community to: – not normalise the erosion of human rights as a cost of security policies and economic development initiatives; – strengthen monitoring and support for human rights defenders and civil society organisations. " The international community cannot look the other way. Ecuador needs strong support to protect those who defend rights. Our organisations will remain vigilant through international oversight and will closely monitor the human rights situation in the country ," emphasised the signatory organisations. body: 28/08/2026 Statement India en fr United Nations FIDH The International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) welcomes the findings and recommendations made by the United Nations (UN) Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination (CERD) related to India. FIDH urges the Indian authorities to fully implement the CERD’s recommendations without delay, particularly regarding comprehensively criminalising discrimination and hate crimes, and ensuring accountability for perpetrators of related human rights violations. Paris, 28 August 2026 . On 25 August 2026, the UN CERD released its findings and recommendations (known as " Concluding Observations ") concerning India, following the review of the country’s combined 20th and 21st periodic reports on the implementation of the International Convention on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination (ICERD), which took place on 11 and 12 August 2026 in Geneva. The CERD monitors the implementation of the ICERD’s provisions by state parties, including India. Some of the CERD’s Concluding Observations reflected information presented by FIDH and partners in two joint reports submitted to the CERD as part of its review of India. For example, the CERD expressed concern over gaps in the Indian legislative framework, including the lack of a comprehensive definition of racial discrimination and the failure to explicitly criminalise all acts of racist hate speech and hate crimes. It also expressed concerns about " reports of widespread racial discrimination, including hate crimes and hate speech " including by politicians. The CERD called on the Indian government to review the legislative framework to address these gaps, and to take effective measures to increase accountability for hate speech and hate crimes. The CERD was " gravely concerned " by reports of widespread human rights violations against ethnic and ethno-religious groups, Indigenous and Tribal Peoples, and non-citizens, including extrajudicial killings, arbitrary detentions, torture, and sexual violence. It called on the Indian authorities to ensure that perpetrators are prosecuted and held accountable. With regards to civic space, the CERD raised concerns over the use of laws such as the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act (FCRA), the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA), the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act (AFSPA) and the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) to stifle the rights to freedom of expression and association, and to silence human rights defenders, including those working to defend the rights of minorities. It recommended that the authorities review those laws and ensure an enabling environment for civil society. The CERD also expressed concerns about, and made recommendations to address, the specific situations for Dalits, Indigenous and Tribal Peoples, nomadic and semi-nomadic tribes, domestic workers, and migrants and asylum seekers. The CERD noted in particular its concerns relating to the deportation and forcible returns of Rohingya asylum seekers, as well as the use of hate speech by politicians and other public figures targeting Rohingya and Bengali-speaking Muslims. Finally, the CERD made recommendations related to the right of freedom of thought, conscience and religion, the right to health, and the National Register of Citizens and Citizenship Amendment Act. body: Share GEO 002 / 0726 / OBS 36 Arbitrary arrest / Arbitrary detention / Transnational repression / Restrictions to freedom of expression Georgia/Azerbaijan 23 July 2026 The Observatory for the Protection of Human Rights Defenders, a partnership of the World Organisation Against Torture (OMCT) and the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH), requests your urgent intervention in the following situation in Azerbaijan and Georgia . Description of the situation: The Observatory has been informed about the arbitrary arrest and detention of Mr Afgan Sadigov in Azerbaijan, following his previous arbitrary arrest and expulsion from Georgia to Azerbaijan in April 2026. Mr Afgan Sadigov is the founder and editor of the regional online media platform Azel.tv, known for its critical reporting on the Azerbaijani government. Azel.tv’s YouTube channel features video reports on local corruption, government misconduct, and citizens’ grievances regarding social injustice. On 8 June 2026, Mr Sadigov’s wife, Sevinch Sadigova , stated that her husband had been detained by several masked persons dressed in civilian clothes in Azerbaijan. On the same day, Mr Sadigov’s lawyer reported that Mr Sadigov had been taken to the Prosecutor’s Office of Azerbaijan, and that he had been presented to a court hearing, at which he was ordered to stay in pre-trial detention until 30 July 2026. This arbitrary arrest and detention of Mr Sadigov in Azerbaijan followed his arbitrary arrest and expulsion from Georgia to Azerbaijan on 4 April 2026, after nearly two years of judicial and administrative proceedings in both countries. In August 2023, Mr Sadigov was accused of extorsion under Articles 182.2.2 and 182.2.4 of the Criminal Code of the Republic of Azerbaijan. On 3 August 2024, Georgian law enforcement officers first detained Mr Sadigov for the purpose of extradition to Azerbaijan. Despite no concrete evidence against Mr Sadigov, Georgian courts accepted Azerbaijan’s request to expel Mr Sadigov and proceeded to allow his extradition. In January 2025, the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) issued binding interim measures prohibiting Mr Sadigov’s expulsion to Azerbaijan, where he was facing criminal proceedings ( see below ). On 1 April 2026, the Prosecutor’s Office of Azerbaijan declared this criminal investigation to be officially terminated and informed Georgian authorities about their decision to discontinue the criminal proceedings against Mr Sadigov , which was followed by an order by the Georgian Ministry of Justice to terminate the expulsion procedures. On t hat basis, the Georgian government argued that Mr Sadigov was no longer at risk of transfer to Azerbaijan and that there was therefore insufficient factual basis for alleged violations of Articles 3 (prohibition of torture) , 6 (right to a fair trial) , and 8 (right to respect for private and family life) of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) . On 3 April 2026, the Tbilisi City Court approved a motion by the Prosecutor’s Office of Georgia to annul the bail, the ban on leaving the country and other interim measures applied against Mr Sadigov. Nonetheless, in the late evening of 4 April 2026 , dozens of officers from the Georgian Ministry of Internal Affairs and emergency response units arrived at Mr Sadigov ’s residential apartment in Tbilisi and arrested him on alleged administrative grounds f ollowing, on the basis of statements that allegedly constituted an “insult of a law enforcement officer ” under Article 173(2) of Georgia’s Code of Administrative Offence s. Following the arrest, Mr Sadigov was subject to a late-night court hearing before the Tbilisi City Court. Even though Georgian authorities were informed of Mr Sadigov’s chosen legal representatives, the Tbilisi City Court appointed him a public lawyer from the Legal Aid Service . On 5 April 2026, Georgian Judge Tornike Kochkiani found him guilty, fined him with 2,000 lari (approximately 743 Euros) and ordered Mr Sadigov’s expulsion to Azerbaijan and a prohibition to enter Georgia for three years. The decision was immediately implemented, and he was expelled through the Georgian-Azerbaijan land border. Upon crossing into Azerbaijan, he was reportedly questioned by the Azerbaijani Migration Service . On 6 April 2026, Mr Ilham Aliyev, President of Azerbaijan, conducted a visit to Tbilisi, Georgia, which raises concerns on whether this process may have been coordinated at a high political level, with the purpose to punish and expel Mr Sadigov back to Azerbaijan, where he might be subjected to further politically motivated persecution. On 10 April 2026, the European Court of Human Rights sent a request to both parties – the applicant, as well as the governments of Georgia and Azerbaijan – to submit additional observations. In particular, the Court raised a new question as to whether, despite the existence of an interim measure, the applicant’s transfer to Azerbaijan constituted a violation of Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. On 30 June 2026, the Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights, Michael O'Flaherty, addressed a letter requesting clarifications regarding the criminal proceedings against Afgan Sadigov, while reiterating his call for the immediate release of all human rights defenders, journalists, and civil society activists detained solely for their legitimate work or for expressing dissenting or critical views. Prior to these developments, Mr Sadigov had been held in expulsion detention for a period of nine months. Throughout this time, none of the instances of the Georgian judiciary suspended or halted the expulsion proceedings, notwithstanding substantiated concerns regarding a real risk of political persecution, as well as torture and other forms of ill-treatment in Azerbaijan. Furthermore, at all judicial levels, the Georgian courts rejected the requests for international protection submitted by Mr Sadigov and his legal representatives. During his detention, Mr Sadigov undertook a 161-day hunger strike, which resulted in a severely deteriorated and life-threatening health condition. Following his release, Mr Sadigov joined the ongoing continuous protests in Tbilisi, and it was in this context that he was subsequently subjected to administrative detention on two occasions and was fined 55 times under restrictive legislative provisions adopted in Georgia concerning freedom of assembly. The Observatory notes that Mr Sadigov’s expulsion from Georgia, carried out in violation of the interim measures imposed by the ECtHR, constitutes a demonstrative breach of the ECtHR’s decision and of the European Convention on Human Rights, including the principle of non-refoulement and the right to a fair trial. The Observatory further notes that cooperation between Azerbaijani and Georgian authorities to arbitrarily detain and extradite Mr Sadigov in reprisal for his legitimate human rights and journalistic activities constitutes an act of transnational repression. The Observatory strongly condemns the arbitrary detention of Mr Sadigov in Azerbaijan and his previous arbitrary arrest and expulsion by the Georgian authorities and calls on Azerbaijan and Georgia to uphold their human rights obligations, including its duty to protect exiled human rights defenders from transnational repression. Please write to the authorities of Georgia , asking them to: Guarantee in all circumstances that human rights defenders, including foreign nationals engaging in legitimate civic activities, can carry out their work without arbitrary interference, harassment, intimidation, restrictions or reprisals. Ensure that international cooperation mechanisms are not used to criminalise legitimate human rights activities, and refrain from collaborating in any form of transnational repression against human rights defenders; Please write to the authorities of Azerbaijan , asking them to: Guarantee in all circumstances the physical integrity and psycholog
title: Georgia/Azerbaijan: Arbitrary detention of journalist Afgan Sadigov in Azerbaijan following his arbitrary arrest and expulsion from Georgia Read more

body: Share KEN 002 / 0726 / OBS 034 Harassment / Surveillance / Intimidation / Kenya 16 July 2026 The Observatory for the Protection of Human Rights Defenders, a partnership of the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) and the World Organisation Against Torture (OMCT), requests your urgent intervention in the following situation in Kenya . Description of the situation: The Observatory has been informed about the harassment, surveillance and intimidation of Ms Diana Gichengo , a Kenyan lawyer and human rights defender and executive Director of the Institute for Social Accountability (TISA). Through her work with TISA, Ms Gichengo promotes transparency, accountability and civic participation in public finance management and has consistently advocated for the protection of civic space and democratic governance. Ms Gichengo also worked with the Kenya Human Rights Commission (KHRC) and Amnesty International Kenya, where she contributed to the promotion and protection of human rights. On 2 July 2026, at least 13 men suspected of being state security officers arrived at TISA's offices in Nairobi in four Subaru vehicles and attempted to gain access to the premises. Operating outside any legal procedure, the men demanded that TISA staff surrender "the lawyer" working at the organisation. The men did not present a judicial warrant or identify the legal basis for their actions. Following the incident, senior management convened an urgent security meeting and resolved to take immediate measures to enhance both the physical and digital security of TISA and its staff. Additional steps were taken to evacuate a member of the Senior Management Team from the offices who was assessed to be at high risk, among other security measures. Since early June 2026, Ms Diana Gichengo has also been subjected to repeated surveillance and intimidation. She has been continuously followed by occupants of tinted Subaru and Toyota Prado vehicles while traveling on routes she regularly uses to and from work. The surveillance began shortly after Ms Gichengo became aware that individuals close to a senior government official had been making inquiries about her in connection with TISA's work on public finance management and accountability. The Observatory notes that these incidents are not isolated and occur amid an increasing pattern of intimidation targeting human rights defenders and civil society organisations in Kenya. On 22 February 2026, Zimbabwean human rights defender and Africa Director of the Open Society Foundations (OSF) Mr Brian Kagoro was denied entry into Kenya, detained for several hours at Jomo Kenyatta International Airport, in Nairobi, and deported without being formally charged and without any explanation. Earlier, on 5 July 2025, Mr Martin Mavenjina, Senior Legal Advisor at the Kenya Human Rights Commission (KHRC), was deported from Kenya and has since been prevented from returning to the country. More recently, following the demonstrations commemorating 25 June 2026, seven human rights defenders, Fredrick Ojiro , Collins Otieno , Muteti Mulinge , Elisha Alam , Michael Ngugi , Christine Lubanga and Davis Luchuma , were arbitrarily arrested, forcibly disappeared and later found in different parts of Nairobi bearing signs of torture. In addition, Abdulaziz Duba Molu , Michael Oloo Osura and Macmillan Kiarie Mugo remain forcibly disappeared after being unlawfully arrested prior to the 25 June commemoration. The Observatory recalls that, as a State Party to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) and the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights (ACHPR), Kenya must respect and ensure the rights to privacy, freedom of expression, freedom of peaceful assembly and freedom of association. The Observatory expresses its utmost concerns over the surveillance, intimidation and harassment of Ms Diana Gichengo, which appear to be linked to her legitimate work promoting transparency, accountability and democratic governance in Kenya. These documented incidents intend to intimidate Ms Gichengo and create a chilling effect on the work of TISA and other civil society organisations working on governance and accountability issues. The Observatory condemns the harassment, surveillance and intimidation of Ms Diana Gichengo, which appear to be solely aimed at hindering her legitimate human rights activities. The Observatory urges the Kenyan authorities to immediately put an end to all acts of intimidation against her and TISA and to ensure that human rights defenders in Kenya are able to carry out their legitimate activities without fear of harassment, intimidation or reprisals. Actions requested: Please write to the authorities of Kenya asking them to: 1. Guarantee in all circumstances the physical integrity and psychological well-being of Ms Diana Gichengo, the staff of TISA, and all human rights defenders in Kenya; 2. Immediately put an end to all acts of surveillance, intimidation and harassment against Ms Diana Gichengo and ensure that no further acts of intimidation are carried out against her or TISA; 3. Ensure that human rights defenders and civil society organisations in Kenya are able to carry out their legitimate activities freely and safely, without fear of surveillance, intimidation, reprisals or any other form of harassment; 4. Comply in all circumstances with Kenya's obligations under international human rights law, in particular the ICCPR and the ACHPR. Addresses • H.E. body: Share UGA 003 / 0726 / OBS 033 Enforced disappearance / Arbitrary arrest / Arbitrary detention / Judicial harassment Uganda 9 July 2026 The Observatory for the Protection of Human Rights Defenders, a partnership of the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) and the World Organisation Against Torture (OMCT), requests your urgent intervention in the following situation in Uganda . Description of the situation: The Observatory has been informed about the enforced disappearance and the arbitrary arrest and detention of Mr. Erias Lukwago, lawyer, human rights defender and President of the People's Front for Freedom (PFF), well known for representing opposition figures and defending fundamental rights, including the rights to due process and a fair trial. On 15 June 2026, heavily armed security operatives arrested Mr. Erias Lukwago at his residence in Wakaliga, a neighbourhood of Kampala, and took him to an undisclosed location. For more than 48 hours, his whereabouts remained unknown. During this period, General Muhoozi Kainerugaba, Chief of Defence Forces and son of President Yoweri Museveni, repeatedly claimed responsibility for Mr. Lukwago's detention through a series of posts on X, stating that he had "captured" him and taken him to his "basement". On 17 June 2026, Mr. Lukwago was transferred to Kira Division Police Station in Wakiso District before being brought before the Buganda Road Chief Magistrate's Court in Kampala, where he was formally charged with « misprision of treason » , a criminal offence consisting of the alleged failure to report knowledge of plans to commit treason and punishable by life imprisonment under Section 25 of the Ugandan Penal Code. Mr. Lukwago denied the charge and has been remanded to Luzira Prison. On 7 July 2026, Mr. Lukwago's application for bail filed on health grounds was rejected, and he remains in detention pending further proceedings. Mr. Lukwago's arrest occurred while he was acting as legal counsel for opposition leader Dr. Kizza Besigye, who is currently facing treason charges. At the time of his arrest, Mr. Lukwago was also preparing to serve court documents on General Muhoozi Kainerugaba in separate legal proceedings brought on behalf of Dr. Besigye concerning repeated public death threats issued by the General through social media. Mr. Lukwago was arrested shortly before carrying out this procedural step. The Observatory is further concerned that, on 22 June 2026, Kenyan lawyer and former Minister of Justice Ms. Martha Karua was denied entry into Uganda upon her arrival at Entebbe International Airport while she was travelling to Uganda to join the legal team representing Mr. Erias Lukwago in the proceedings against him. The Observatory notes with deep concern that, following Mr. Lukwago's arrest, General Muhoozi Kainerugaba continued publishing threatening statements on X, including: "I'm proud of ALL the hurt and pain I will inflict on the CRIMINAL LUKWAGO!", "Lukwago will be in prison for a minimum of 10 years!", and "He has been fighting me with Besigye for many decades. We are going to finish it now." Such statements seriously undermine the presumption of innocence, appear to interfere with the administration of justice, and reinforce concerns that the arrest and prosecution are politicaly motivated. The Observatory recalls that Mr. Lukwago is a prominent lawyer who has long represented opposition leaders, journalists, human rights defenders and other individuals in politically sensitive cases involving the protection of fundamental rights and freedoms. The Observatory expresses its utmost concern that his arbitrary arrest, detention and prosecution appear to be directly linked to his legitimate professional activities as a lawyer and his human rights work. The Observatory further recalls that another of Dr. Besigye's lawyers, Mr. Eron Kiiza , was arbitrarily arrested in January 2025, convicted by a military court for alleged contempt of court and sentenced to nine months' imprisonment before being released on bail in February 2025. These successive incidents raise serious concerns about an emerging pattern of intimidation and judicial harassment targeting lawyers representing opposition figures in Uganda. The Observatory condemns the enforced desappearance, arbitrary arrest and detention and the judicial harassment of Mr. Erias Lukwago, which appear to be solely aimed at punishing him for his legitimate activities as a lawyer. The Observatory further condemns the public threats and statements made by General Muhoozi Kainerugaba before and after Mr. Lukwago's arrest, which raise serious concerns regarding the independence of the proceedings against him and the respect for the rule of law in Uganda. The Observatory urges the Ugandan authorities to immediately and unconditionally release Mr. Erias Lukwago, drop all charges against him, and guarantee in all circumstances that lawyers and human rights defenders in Uganda are able to carry out their legitimate activities without fear of reprisals, intimidation or judicial harassment. Actions requested: Please write to the Ugandan authorities urging them to: i. Guarantee in all circumstances the physical integrity and psychological well-being of Erias Lukwago, and all human rights defenders in Uganda; ii. Immediately and unconditionally release Erias Lukwago and drop all charges against him as his detention appears to be solely linked to his legitimate activities as a lawyer and human rights defender; iii. Put an end to all acts of harassment, including at the judicial level, against Mr. Erias Lukwago, and all human rights defenders, lawyers and political opponents in Uganda, and ensure that they are able to carry out their legitimate activities without fear of reprisals, intimidation or judicial harassment; Addresses: • Mr Kaguta Yoweri Museveni, President of the Republic of Uganda, E-mail: [email protected] / [email protected] , X: @KagutaMuseveni • Ms Robinah Nabbanja, Prime Minister of the Republic of Uganda, Email: [email protected] , X: @RobinahNabbanja • Mr Jeje Odongo Abubakher, Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Uganda, X: @UgandaMFA • Hon.
